docs.title: pyresilience
docs.text:
Unified resilience patterns for Python — retry, circuit breaker, timeout, fallback, bulkhead, rate limiter, and cache in one decorator.

Instead of stacking multiple decorators from different libraries, define your entire resilience policy in a single @resilient() call.

docs.title: Why pyresilience?
docs.text:
Existing Python libraries solve individual problems well:

  • tenacity — retry only
  • pybreaker — circuit breaker only
  • wrapt_timeout_decorator — timeout only

But combining them means stacking decorators, managing separate configs, and losing visibility across patterns. pyresilience unifies everything.

docs.title: All Seven Patterns
docs.text: Module Config Description Circuit Breaker CircuitBreakerConfig Prevents calls to failing services Retry RetryConfig Retries failed calls with backoff Bulkhead BulkheadConfig Limits concurrent executions Timeout TimeoutConfig Enforces per-call time limits Rate Limiter RateLimiterConfig Limits call rate per time window Cache CacheConfig Caches successful results Fallback FallbackConfig Graceful degradation on failure

docs.title: At a Glance
docs.text:
import requests
from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig, TimeoutConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, delay=1.0),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=10),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
)
def call_payment_api(amount: float) -> dict:
    return requests.post("/charge", json={"amount": amount}).json()

This single decorator:

  1. Retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff
  2. Times out each attempt after 10 seconds
  3. Opens the circuit after 5 consecutive failures, blocking further calls until recovery

All patterns work together, with a unified event system for observability.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• All 7 resilience patterns in one library
  • One decorator — @resilient() combines everything
  • Zero dependencies — pure Python stdlib
  • Full async support — auto-detects sync vs async
  • Type-safe — strict mypy compatible, py.typed marker
  • Sliding window circuit breaker — failure rate % threshold, slow call detection
  • Retry on result — retry based on return values, not just exceptions
  • Retry budget — shared token pool limits cascading retries across callers
  • Composable timeouts — per-attempt limit, overall deadline, or both, plus a stream idle timeout
  • LLM-grade rate limiting — several limits at once, weighted calls, token reconciliation, limits that follow Retry-After and rate-limit headers
  • Fallback alternatives with cooldown — route a failing call to another provider and skip the one that is down
  • Shared state — one circuit breaker, rate limit and retry budget across processes through a pluggable backend (in-memory, Redis)
  • Context propagation — request-scoped metadata in every event via resilience_context
  • Opinionated presets — http_policy(), db_policy(), queue_policy(), strict_policy(), llm_policy()
  • Production observability — JSON logging, metrics, OpenTelemetry spans, Prometheus counters/histograms
  • Health check — inspect circuit breaker states, in-flight calls, rate limiter availability
  • Graceful shutdown — drain in-flight calls with configurable timeout
  • Optional performance backends — uvloop + orjson
  • Python 3.9+ — CI tests 3.10 through 3.15 on Linux, macOS and Windows
  • Production/Stable — 863 tests, 98% branch coverage, 10.4x faster than tenacity

docs.title: Why Not Just Tenacity + PyBreaker?
docs.text:
With separate libraries, you end up stacking decorators that don't share state:

# Three libraries, three configs, no coordination
from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential
from pybreaker import CircuitBreaker
from wrapt_timeout_decorator import timeout

breaker = CircuitBreaker(fail_max=5)

@timeout(10)
@breaker
@retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), wait=wait_exponential())
def call_api():
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com/data").json()
# No fallback. No rate limiting. No caching. No shared metrics.
# The circuit breaker doesn't know about retries. Timeouts don't coordinate with backoff.

With pyresilience, everything is coordinated through one decorator:

import requests
from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig, TimeoutConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig
from pyresilience import FallbackConfig, RateLimiterConfig, CacheConfig

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, delay=1.0),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=10),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(handler=lambda e: {"error": "service unavailable"}),
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=100, period=60.0),
    cache=CacheConfig(max_size=256, ttl=300.0),
)
def call_api():
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com/data").json()
# One decorator. All patterns. Shared state. Unified metrics.

The circuit breaker counts retried failures correctly. Rate limiting respects bulkhead limits. Cache short-circuits the entire pipeline. One event system observes everything.

docs.title: Observability at a Glance
docs.text:
Every resilience event — retries, circuit state changes, rate limit hits — can be observed with listeners:

from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig
from pyresilience import JsonEventLogger, MetricsCollector, EventType

logger = JsonEventLogger()
metrics = MetricsCollector()

def alert_on_circuit_open(event):
    if event.event_type == EventType.CIRCUIT_OPEN:
        print(f"ALERT: Circuit opened for {event.function_name}")

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    listeners=[logger, metrics, alert_on_circuit_open],
)
def payment_service(amount: float):
    return process_payment(amount)

# After some calls, check metrics:
# metrics.summary() -> {"total_events": 150, "success_rate": 0.95, ...}

See Observability for the full event system, JSON logging, and metrics collection.

docs.title: FastAPI Integration
docs.text:
Use pyresilience with FastAPI's dependency injection for per-route resilience:

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from pyresilience import ResilienceConfig, RetryConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig
from pyresilience.contrib.fastapi import ResilientDependency

app = FastAPI()

payment_resilience = ResilientDependency(ResilienceConfig(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
))

@app.post("/charge")
async def charge(
    amount: float,
    resilience: ResilientDependency = Depends(payment_resilience),
):
    return await resilience.call(payment_service.charge, amount)

Also supports Django and Flask.

docs.title: resilient
docs.text:
The main decorator that applies resilience patterns.

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(...),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(...),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(...),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(...),
    bulkhead=BulkheadConfig(...),
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(...),
    cache=CacheConfig(...),
    retry_budget=RetryBudgetConfig(...),
    listeners=[...],
    shared_state=SharedStateConfig(...),
)

Can also be used bare: @resilient applies default retry (3 attempts).

docs.title: resilience_context
docs.text:
A contextvars.ContextVar[Optional[dict]] that carries request-scoped metadata into every ResilienceEvent.context field.

from pyresilience import resilience_context

resilience_context.set({"trace_id": "abc-123"})

docs.title: shutdown()
docs.text:
Drains in-flight calls and releases thread pool resources. Call during application shutdown.

from pyresilience import shutdown

shutdown()

docs.title: get_in_flight_count()
docs.text:
Returns the number of currently executing resilient calls. Requires enable_in_flight_tracking() to be called first.

from pyresilience import enable_in_flight_tracking, get_in_flight_count

enable_in_flight_tracking()
# ... after some calls are in progress ...
count = get_in_flight_count()

docs.title: enable_in_flight_tracking()
docs.text: Activates in-flight call counting. Disabled by default to avoid overhead. Once enabled, get_in_flight_count() returns accurate counts.

docs.title: health_check(registry)
docs.text:
Returns a dict summarizing resilience state for all registered functions in a ResilienceRegistry.

from pyresilience import ResilienceRegistry, health_check

status = health_check(registry)
# {"payment-api": {"circuit_breaker": "closed", "in_flight": 3, ...}, ...}

docs.title: db_policy(**kwargs)

docs.title: queue_policy(**kwargs)

docs.title: strict_policy(**kwargs)

docs.title: llm_policy(**kwargs)
docs.text: Optimized for LLM / HTTP API calls: 60s timeout, 4 attempts with 429-aware Retry-After-honoring backoff, client-side rate limiter (60 calls/60s), circuit breaker at 5 failures. Optional tokens_per_minute (with token_cost / token_usage), adaptive_rate_limit and rate_limit_max_wait. See HTTP & LLM Helpers.

docs.text: Stdlib-only helpers in pyresilience.contrib.http (not re-exported from the package root):

docs.title: retry_on_status(*codes)
docs.text: Returns a predicate for RetryConfig.retry_on_result. Duck-typed: matches integer status_code (requests/httpx) or status (aiohttp) attributes against codes.

docs.title: retry_after_delay(max_wait=60.0)
docs.text: Returns a delay_func for RetryConfig.delay_func. Parses the Retry-After header (delta-seconds and HTTP-date forms) from the triggering response or from an exception carrying a .response attribute; returns None (exponential backoff fallback) when absent or unparseable; result is clamped to [0, max_wait].

docs.title: rate_limit_feedback(*, calls_limit="calls", tokens_limit="tokens", max_pause=60.0)
docs.text: Returns a feedback function for RateLimiterConfig.feedback. Parses Retry-After, x-ratelimit-*, anthropic-ratelimit-* and RateLimit-* headers from a response or from an exception carrying a .response, and returns a RateLimitFeedback (or None). Pauses are capped at max_pause seconds.

docs.title: New Features
docs.text:
• Composable timeouts: TimeoutConfig.total_seconds adds an overall deadline for all attempts and retry waits on top of the per-attempt seconds; each attempt gets min(seconds, time left). See TimeLimiter
  • Stream idle timeout: TimeoutConfig.stream_idle_seconds bounds the wait for the first item and between items of an iterator or async iterator result
  • Several rate limits at once: RateLimiterConfig.limits with RateLimit entries, acquired all-or-nothing (requests and tokens, per second and per day). See RateLimiter
  • Weighted rate limiting: cost computes a call's weight from its arguments
  • Token reconciliation: actual_cost settles the reserved estimate against the real usage after the call
  • Server-driven rate limiting: RateLimiterConfig.feedback and RateLimitFeedback; contrib.http.rate_limit_feedback() parses Retry-After, x-ratelimit-*, anthropic-ratelimit-* and RateLimit-* headers
  • charge_retries: debit every retry attempt against the limits
  • llm_policy() options: tokens_per_minute, token_cost, token_usage, adaptive_rate_limit, rate_limit_max_wait (defaults unchanged)
  • Fallback alternatives: FallbackConfig.alternatives are tried in order with the original arguments before the handler. See Fallback
  • Fallback cooldown: cooldown and cooldown_threshold skip a target that keeps failing; new EventType.COOLDOWN
  • Shared state across processes: SharedStateConfig with a pluggable StateBackend shares circuit breaker, rate limit and retry budget state; InMemoryBackend in the core, contrib.redis.RedisBackend around a Redis client you supply. Still zero dependencies. Works in forked workers, and during a backend outage one call at a time waits for the backend instead of every call. See Shared State
  • Python 3.15: supported and tested in CI

docs.title: Changes
docs.text:
• Registry: sync and async functions under one name now share the circuit breaker, rate limits, retry budget and fallback cooldown state (bulkhead slots and cached results stay separate per call style)
  • Total-deadline timeouts stop retrying as soon as the time left cannot cover the next retry wait and raise ResilienceTimeoutError chained from the last error, instead of sleeping through the remaining waits. A fallback for the error that was being retried still applies
  • Rate limit rejections name the limit in the event detail and error message when cost, limits, feedback or charge_retries is configured

docs.title: Bug Fixes
docs.text: • Retry budget for retry_on_result: result-triggered retries now consume the shared retry budget in both sync and async executors, matching the existing behavior for exception retries. When the budget is exhausted the latest result is returned and a RETRY_EXHAUSTED event is emitted. Previously retry_on_result retries bypassed the budget entirely.

docs.title: New Features
docs.text:
• ignore_on: RetryConfig.ignore_on and CircuitBreakerConfig.ignore_on list exception types that are never retried and never counted as circuit failures — takes precedence over retry_on/error_types and bypasses fallback, so terminal client errors (auth, quota, validation) fail fast
  • delay_func: RetryConfig.delay_func computes the per-attempt delay from the triggering exception or retry_on_result value; return None to fall back to exponential backoff. Returns are clamped to [0, max_delay]
  • pyresilience.contrib.http: stdlib-only helpers, duck-typed for requests/httpx/aiohttp — retry_on_status() predicate for retry_on_result, and retry_after_delay() which parses Retry-After headers (delta-seconds and HTTP-date) from responses or exceptions carrying .response
  • llm_policy() preset: client-side rate limiter + 429-aware, Retry-After-honoring retry + timeout + circuit breaker tuned for LLM/HTTP APIs; exported from the package root

docs.text: • New config fields cost ≤ +0.07μs on the retry happy path; two new bench_overhead.py cases track ignore_on/delay_func overhead permanently

docs.title: New Features
docs.text:
• Context propagation: resilience_context ContextVar carries request-scoped metadata (trace ID, user ID, etc.) into every ResilienceEvent.context field automatically
  • Per-attempt timeout: TimeoutConfig(per_attempt=False) enforces a single deadline across all retry attempts instead of resetting per attempt
  • Retry budget: RetryBudgetConfig(max_retries=100, refill_rate=10) provides a shared token pool that prevents cascading retries across decorated functions
  • Health check: health_check(registry) returns a dict summarizing circuit breaker states, in-flight calls, and rate limiter availability for all registered functions
  • OpenTelemetry listener: OpenTelemetryListener emits spans and attributes for each resilience event, integrating with the OpenTelemetry SDK
  • Prometheus listener: PrometheusListener exports counters and histograms to Prometheus via the official client library
  • Graceful shutdown: shutdown() drains in-flight calls and releases thread pool resources cleanly
  • Event duration tracking: ResilienceEvent.duration field populated on SUCCESS events for observability integrations
  • Production/Stable classifier: PyPI classifier bumped to Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable

docs.title: Bug Fixes
docs.text:
• AsyncResultCache.put() race condition: Fixed unsafe read of _store.keys() without holding the lock; ResultCache.put() now returns evicted keys directly
  • Prometheus histogram unused: PrometheusListener now observes call duration via _duration_histogram on SUCCESS events
  • Cache lock memory leak: Per-key locks in cache stampede prevention are now evicted alongside their cache entries, preventing unbounded lock accumulation
  • asyncio.iscoroutinefunction deprecation: Replaced remaining usage with inspect.iscoroutinefunction for Python 3.14+ compatibility
  • install_uvloop deprecated API: Switched from uvloop.install() to uvloop.EventLoopPolicy() to silence deprecation warnings
  • Registry executor exposure: ResilienceRegistry now exposes executors via get_executor(name) for runtime introspection without private attribute access

  • Duration timing gated behind if has_listeners: — zero cost on hot path
  • Lazy in-flight tracking: counter and lock only allocated when enable_in_flight_tracking() is called
  • Benchmark results (Apple Silicon): 0.64μs decorator overhead, 223,934 ops/sec throughput, 14.4x faster than tenacity async

docs.title: New Features
docs.text:
• Circuit breaker manual control: Added reset(), force_open(), force_close() methods to CircuitBreaker for operational needs (maintenance windows, graceful degradation)
  • Async fallback handlers: FallbackConfig.handler can now be an async function when used with async decorated functions. Detected via asyncio.iscoroutinefunction
  • Cache stampede prevention: Per-key locking with double-check pattern prevents thundering herd on cache miss. Only one thread/coroutine computes per cache key; others wait for the result
  • Sync timeout thread cancellation: Uses ctypes.pythonapi.PyThreadState_SetAsyncExc for best-effort thread interruption on CPython. Exception chain preserved (from exc). Will not interrupt blocking C extensions
  • AsyncBulkhead loop safety: Detects event loop changes and recreates semaphore automatically. Safe across multiple asyncio.run() calls

docs.title: Bug Fixes
docs.text:
• FallbackConfig default constructor: FallbackConfig() now works without arguments. When handler=None, fallback_on is auto-cleared to () to prevent silently returning None on exceptions
  • Circuit breaker race condition: Removed lock-free fast path in allow_request() — always acquires lock. Safe for free-threaded Python 3.13+ (--disable-gil)
  • Circuit breaker re-checked between retries: CB state is verified before each retry attempt. If the CB opened (from other threads), retries stop immediately with CircuitOpenError
  • MetricsCollector async collision: Replaced threading.get_ident() with contextvars.ContextVar — concurrent async coroutines no longer corrupt latency tracking
  • Jitter zero-delay floor: Jitter now has a 10% minimum floor (max(base * 0.1, random() * delay)), preventing zero-delay retry storms
  • Timeout exception chaining: ResilienceTimeoutError now chains via from exc instead of from None, preserving original traceback for debugging
  • strict_policy docstring: Corrected from "1 retry (2 total attempts)" to "No retries (1 total attempt)"
  • Django max_retries → max_attempts: Config key renamed for consistency with RetryConfig. Old key still works with DeprecationWarning
  • mypy clean: Fixed uvloop/orjson import errors via pyproject.toml overrides. mypy now passes with zero errors

docs.title: Improvements
docs.text:
• Bulkhead released during retry sleep: Bulkhead slot is now released during retry backoff and reacquired before the next attempt, preventing slot starvation
  • Cooperative timeout cancel: Sync timeout uses threading.Event for cancel signaling instead of no-op future.cancel()
  • Listener errors logged: Broken listeners now emit logging.warning() instead of being silently swallowed
  • Bounded MetricsCollector memory: Latency history bounded to 10,000 entries via collections.deque(maxlen=10000)
  • Larger default thread pool: Sync timeout pool increased from 4 to min(32, cpu_count + 4) workers
  • Decorator introspection: Wrapped functions now expose _executor attribute for runtime access to circuit breaker, cache, etc.
  • Config validation: FallbackConfig and CacheConfig now validate inputs in __post_init__
  • BulkheadFullError import cleanup: Now imported directly from _exceptions module

docs.title: Combining Patterns
docs.text: One of pyresilience's key advantages is combining multiple resilience patterns in a single decorator with a well-defined execution order.

docs.title: Execution Order
docs.text:
When multiple patterns are configured, they execute in this order:

Incoming call
     |
     v
 [1. Cache] ──── hit? ──> return cached result
     |
     miss
     |
     v
 [2. Circuit Breaker] ──── open? ──> reject / fallback
     |
     closed/half-open
     |
     v
 [3. Rate Limiter] ──── exceeded? ──> reject / fallback
     |
     allowed
     |
     v
 [4. Bulkhead] ──── full? ──> reject / fallback
     |
     slot acquired
     |
     v
 [5. Retry Loop]
     |
     v
 [6. Timeout] ──── exceeded? ──> TimeoutError (may retry)
     |
     v
 [7. Function Call]
     |
     v
 Store in cache (if configured)
     |
     v
 Return result

docs.title: Why This Order?
docs.text:
1. Cache first — avoid unnecessary work entirely
  2. Circuit breaker — fail fast if the dependency is known to be down
  3. Rate limiter — respect upstream rate limits before consuming resources
  4. Bulkhead — protect local resources (connections, threads)
  5. Retry — handle transient failures within the protected scope
  6. Timeout — each retry attempt gets its own timeout

docs.title: HTTP API Client
docs.text:
@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, delay=0.5, backoff_factor=2.0),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=10),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(handler=lambda e: {"error": str(e)}),
)
def call_api(endpoint: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(endpoint).json()

    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=10),

async def call_third_party_api(query: str) -> dict:
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get(f"https://api.example.com/search?q={query}") as resp:
            return await resp.json()

@resilient(
    cache=CacheConfig(max_size=256, ttl=300.0),
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, delay=0.5, backoff_factor=2.0, jitter=True),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=10),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30),
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=100, period=60.0),
    bulkhead=BulkheadConfig(max_concurrent=20),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(handler=lambda e: None),
    listeners=[JsonEventLogger(), MetricsCollector()],
)
def mission_critical_call(request_id: str) -> dict:
    return requests.post("https://api.example.com/process", json={"id": request_id}).json()

docs.title: Fallback Behavior
docs.text:
The fallback is checked when:

  • The circuit breaker is open
  • The rate limiter rejects a call
  • The bulkhead is full
  • All retries are exhausted
  • The overall deadline (total_seconds) is spent
  • A non-retryable exception occurs

A fallback can be a value, a handler, or a list of alternatives that receive the original arguments, with an optional cooldown for targets that keep failing. See Fallback.

docs.title: Default Constructor
docs.text:
FallbackConfig() works without arguments. When handler=None, fallback_on is auto-cleared to (), so no exceptions are silently swallowed:

# Safe — no fallback is actually triggered (fallback_on is empty)
@resilient(fallback=FallbackConfig())
def my_func(): ...

docs.title: Sync Fallback
docs.text:
from pyresilience import (
    FallbackConfig,
    BulkheadFullError,
    RateLimitExceededError,
)

@resilient(
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=10, period=1.0),
    bulkhead=BulkheadConfig(max_concurrent=5),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(
        handler=lambda e: {"status": "degraded", "reason": type(e).__name__},
        fallback_on=(Exception, BulkheadFullError, RateLimitExceededError),
    ),
)
def resilient_call() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

docs.title: Async Fallback Handlers
docs.text:
The fallback handler can be an async function when used with async decorated functions. pyresilience detects this via asyncio.iscoroutinefunction and awaits it automatically:

async def fetch_from_backup(exc: Exception) -> dict:
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get("https://backup-api.example.com/data") as resp:
            return await resp.json()

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(
        handler=fetch_from_backup,
        fallback_on=(Exception,),
    ),
)
async def fetch_data() -> dict:
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get("https://primary-api.example.com/data") as resp:
            return await resp.json()

docs.title: Retry + Circuit Breaker
docs.text:
Each failed attempt counts toward the circuit breaker's failure threshold:

Attempt 1: ConnectionError → circuit records failure (1/5)
Attempt 2: ConnectionError → circuit records failure (2/5)
Attempt 3: ConnectionError → circuit records failure (3/5)
(retries exhausted)

Next call:
Attempt 1: ConnectionError → circuit records failure (4/5)
...

docs.title: Cache + Retry
docs.text:
Cache hits bypass the entire retry/timeout/circuit breaker pipeline:

Call 1: CACHE_MISS → execute (with retries) → SUCCESS → store in cache
Call 2: CACHE_HIT → return immediately (no retries needed)

docs.title: Timeout + Retry
docs.text:
Each retry attempt gets its own timeout:

Attempt 1: [──── 10s timeout ────] TIMEOUT
Attempt 2: [──── 10s timeout ────] TIMEOUT
Attempt 3: [── 3s ──] SUCCESS

Total worst case: max_attempts * timeout + (max_attempts - 1) * max_delay

docs.title: Framework Integrations
docs.text: pyresilience provides built-in integrations for the most popular Python web frameworks.

docs.title: Dependency Injection (Recommended)
docs.text:
Use ResilientDependency with FastAPI's Depends() for per-route resilience:

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from pyresilience import ResilienceConfig, RetryConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig
from pyresilience.contrib.fastapi import ResilientDependency

app = FastAPI()

# Create a resilience dependency for the payment service
payment_resilience = ResilientDependency(ResilienceConfig(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
))

@app.post("/charge")
async def charge(
    amount: float,
    resilience: ResilientDependency = Depends(payment_resilience),
):
    return await resilience.call(payment_service.charge, amount)

@app.post("/refund")
async def refund(
    amount: float,
    resilience: ResilientDependency = Depends(payment_resilience),
):
    return await resilience.call(payment_service.refund, amount)

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pyresilience import ResilienceConfig, TimeoutConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig

from pyresilience.contrib.fastapi import resilient_dependency

from pyresilience.contrib.django import resilient_view

Apply resilience to your entire Flask app:

from flask import Flask
from pyresilience import ResilienceConfig, TimeoutConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig
from pyresilience.contrib.flask import Resilience

app = Flask(__name__)
resilience = Resilience(app, config=ResilienceConfig(

@app.route("/data")
def get_data():

docs.text:
from pyresilience.contrib.flask import resilient_route
from pyresilience import RetryConfig, TimeoutConfig

@app.route("/data")
@resilient_route(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),

docs.title: Using Without Integrations
docs.text:
You can always use pyresilience directly with any framework:

from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3))
async def my_service_call():
    return await http_client.get("/api/data")

The framework integrations are convenience wrappers — the core @resilient() decorator works everywhere.

Async Fallback Handlers

When using async frameworks (FastAPI, async Django), your FallbackConfig.handler can be an async function. pyresilience detects this automatically and awaits the handler:

async def async_fallback(exc: Exception) -> dict:
    return {"status": "degraded", "error": str(exc)}

@resilient(
    fallback=FallbackConfig(handler=async_fallback, fallback_on=(Exception,)),
)
async def my_endpoint():
    return await external_service.call()

docs.title: HTTP & LLM Helpers
docs.text:
pyresilience.contrib.http provides stdlib-only building blocks for the most common resilience need on the internet today: handling HTTP 429 rate limits and Retry-After headers when calling REST and LLM APIs.

The helpers are duck-typed — they work with requests, httpx, and aiohttp response objects without importing any of them. The module has zero dependencies beyond the Python standard library, so the core package's zero-deps promise holds.

from pyresilience.contrib.http import retry_on_status, retry_after_delay

Note

These helpers live under pyresilience.contrib.http and are not re-exported from the package root, matching the other contrib integrations. The llm_policy() preset wires them up for you.

docs.title: retry_on_status(*codes)
docs.text:
Builds a predicate for RetryConfig.retry_on_result that returns True when a response's status code matches one of codes.

from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig
from pyresilience.contrib.http import retry_on_status

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(
    max_attempts=4,
    retry_on_result=retry_on_status(429, 500, 502, 503, 504),
))
def call_api():
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com/data")   # don't raise_for_status()

Behavior:

  • Reads response.status_code (requests/httpx) first, then response.status (aiohttp).
  • Only genuine integers match — strings like "429" and bool values are rejected.
  • Returns False for anything that isn't response-shaped, so it's safe with mixed return types.
  • Raises ValueError when called with no codes and TypeError for non-integer codes.

docs.title: retry_after_delay(max_wait=60.0)
docs.text:
Builds a delay_func that reads the Retry-After header from the object that triggered the retry and waits exactly as long as the server asked — instead of guessing with exponential backoff.

from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig
from pyresilience.contrib.http import retry_on_status, retry_after_delay

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(
    max_attempts=4,
    delay=1.0,                                   # backoff base when no Retry-After is present
    retry_on_result=retry_on_status(429, 503),
    delay_func=retry_after_delay(max_wait=60.0),
))
def call_api():
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com/data")

Behavior:

  • Header sources, in order: trigger.headers, then trigger.response.headers (covers requests.HTTPError-shaped exceptions raised by raise_for_status()).
  • Parses both Retry-After forms: delta-seconds ("30") and HTTP-date ("Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT").
  • Returns None when the header is missing or unparseable — pyresilience then falls back to the configured exponential backoff. Your retries never break because of a weird header.
  • The returned delay is clamped to [0, max_wait], so a misbehaving server can't make your client sleep for an hour.
  • Raises ValueError at build time when max_wait <= 0.

docs.title: rate_limit_feedback()
docs.text:
A feedback function for RateLimiterConfig.feedback. It reads the headers of each attempt's response, or of the response attached to a raised exception, and tells the client-side limiter what the server reported:

from pyresilience import resilient, RateLimit, RateLimiterConfig
from pyresilience.contrib.http import rate_limit_feedback

@resilient(
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(
        max_calls=60,
        period=60.0,
        limits=[RateLimit(90_000, 60.0, name="tokens", cost=lambda prompt: len(prompt) // 4)],
        feedback=rate_limit_feedback(),
    ),
)
def ask_model(prompt: str):
    return http_client.post(url, json={"input": prompt})
Header Effect Retry-After (seconds or HTTP-date) Pause the limiter x-ratelimit-remaining-requests, anthropic-ratelimit-requests-remaining, x-ratelimit-remaining, RateLimit-Remaining Lower the request limit to the reported value x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens, anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-remaining Lower the token limit to the reported value matching *-reset header, when the remaining value is 0 Pause until the reset

Reset values may be seconds from now, an epoch timestamp, a duration such as 6m0s or 20ms, an RFC 3339 timestamp or an HTTP-date.

Parameter Default Description calls_limit "calls" Name of the limit that counts requests (the primary limit) tokens_limit "tokens" Name of the limit that counts tokens max_pause 60.0 Upper bound in seconds for any pause

Headers are matched case-insensitively, also in plain dicts. Missing or unparseable headers are ignored, and the function never raises.

docs.title: Putting It Together for LLM APIs
docs.text:
For OpenAI/Anthropic-style clients that raise exceptions on 429 instead of returning responses, attach the helpers to the exception side — retry_after_delay already understands exceptions carrying a .response attribute:

from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig
from pyresilience.contrib.http import retry_after_delay

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(
        max_attempts=4,
        delay=1.0,
        retry_on=(RateLimitError, APIConnectionError),   # retryable
        ignore_on=(AuthenticationError, PermissionDeniedError),  # terminal: fail fast
        delay_func=retry_after_delay(max_wait=60.0),
    ),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(
        failure_threshold=5,
        ignore_on=(AuthenticationError, PermissionDeniedError),  # don't trip the circuit
    ),
)
def ask_model(prompt: str):
    return client.chat.completions.create(model="...", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])

Or skip the wiring entirely with the llm_policy() preset, which combines all of the above with a client-side rate limiter:

from pyresilience import resilient, llm_policy

@resilient(**llm_policy(ignore_on=(AuthenticationError,)))
def ask_model(prompt: str): ...

With token limits and server feedback:

@resilient(**llm_policy(
    max_calls=60,                                   # requests per minute
    tokens_per_minute=90_000,
    token_cost=lambda prompt: len(prompt) // 4 + 256,          # estimate, reserved up front
    token_usage=lambda response: response.usage.total_tokens,  # settled after the call
    adaptive_rate_limit=True,                       # follow Retry-After and x-ratelimit-* headers
    rate_limit_max_wait=10.0,                       # wait up to 10s for capacity
))
def ask_model(prompt: str): ...

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: pyresilience provides a unified event system for monitoring all resilience patterns. Every retry, timeout, circuit state change, and rejection emits an event that you can observe, log, and measure.

docs.title: Event System
docs.text:
Every resilience action emits a ResilienceEvent:

from pyresilience import ResilienceEvent, EventType

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ResilienceEvent:
    event_type: EventType        # What happened
    function_name: str           # Which function
    attempt: int = 0             # Current attempt number
    error: BaseException = None  # The exception, if any
    detail: str = ""             # Additional context
    context: Optional[dict] = None  # Request-scoped metadata (from resilience_context)
    duration: Optional[float] = None  # Call duration in seconds (set on SUCCESS events)

docs.title: Event Types
docs.text: Event When Emitted RETRY A retry attempt is about to be made RETRY_EXHAUSTED All retry attempts have been used TIMEOUT A call exceeded its time limit CIRCUIT_OPEN Circuit breaker opened or rejected a call CIRCUIT_HALF_OPEN Circuit breaker entered half-open state CIRCUIT_CLOSED Circuit breaker closed (recovered) FALLBACK_USED A fallback value was returned COOLDOWN A fallback target entered cooldown after repeated failures BULKHEAD_REJECTED A call was rejected by the bulkhead RATE_LIMITED A call was rejected by the rate limiter CACHE_HIT A cached result was returned CACHE_MISS No cache entry found SUCCESS The call succeeded FAILURE The call failed (non-retryable or exhausted) SLOW_CALL A call exceeded the slow call duration threshold

docs.title: Context Propagation
docs.text:
Use resilience_context to attach request-scoped metadata to every event. This is useful for correlating resilience events with traces, users, or requests.

from pyresilience import resilience_context

# Set context for the current async task / thread
resilience_context.set({"trace_id": "abc-123", "user_id": "u-456"})

# All events emitted during this context will include:
# event.context == {"trace_id": "abc-123", "user_id": "u-456"}

In a web framework, set the context in middleware:

@app.middleware("http")
async def add_resilience_context(request, call_next):
    resilience_context.set({
        "trace_id": request.headers.get("x-trace-id"),
        "path": request.url.path,
    })
    return await call_next(request)

docs.title: Custom Listeners
docs.text:
A listener is any callable that accepts a ResilienceEvent:

from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig, ResilienceEvent

def my_listener(event: ResilienceEvent) -> None:
    print(f"[{event.event_type.value}] {event.function_name} "
          f"attempt={event.attempt} {event.detail}")

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
    listeners=[my_listener],
)
def my_function():
    return do_work()

You can attach multiple listeners:

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
    listeners=[logger, metrics, alerter],
)
def critical_function():
    ...

Note

Listener exceptions are logged as warnings (via logging.warning()) to prevent broken observability from being silently swallowed, while still protecting the application from listener failures.

docs.title: JsonEventLogger
docs.text:
Structured JSON logging out of the box:

from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig, JsonEventLogger

logger = JsonEventLogger()  # Uses Python's logging module

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3), listeners=[logger])
def my_function():
    return do_work()

Output:

{"event_type": "retry", "function_name": "my_function", "attempt": 1, "detail": "retrying in 1.00s", "error_type": "ConnectionError", "error_message": "Connection refused"}
{"event_type": "success", "function_name": "my_function", "attempt": 2}

docs.title: Custom Logger
docs.text:
import logging

my_logger = logging.getLogger("resilience")
json_logger = JsonEventLogger(logger=my_logger, level=logging.WARNING)

def my_function():

Export metrics to Prometheus, Datadog, etc.:

from pyresilience import MetricsCollector

metrics = MetricsCollector()

@app.get("/metrics")

docs.title: Alerting Example
docs.text:
from pyresilience import EventType

def alert_on_circuit_open(event):
    if event.event_type == EventType.CIRCUIT_OPEN:
        send_slack_alert(
            f"Circuit breaker opened for {event.function_name}: {event.error}"
        )
    elif event.event_type == EventType.CIRCUIT_CLOSED:
        send_slack_alert(
            f"Circuit breaker recovered for {event.function_name}"
        )

@resilient(
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    listeners=[json_logger, metrics, alert_on_circuit_open],
)
def payment_service():
    ...

docs.title: OpenTelemetry
docs.text:
OpenTelemetryListener emits spans and attributes for each resilience event, integrating with the OpenTelemetry SDK.

from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig
from pyresilience.contrib.otel import OpenTelemetryListener

otel = OpenTelemetryListener()

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3), listeners=[otel])
def call_api():
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

Each event creates a span with attributes like resilience.event_type, resilience.function_name, resilience.attempt, and resilience.context.* (from resilience_context).

Note

Requires the opentelemetry-api package. Install with pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-sdk.

docs.title: Prometheus
docs.text:
PrometheusListener exports counters and histograms to Prometheus via the official client library.

from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig
from pyresilience.contrib.prometheus import PrometheusListener

prom = PrometheusListener(namespace="myapp")

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3), listeners=[prom])
def call_api():
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

Exported metrics:

Metric Type Labels Description myapp_events_total Counter event_type, function_name Total events by type and function myapp_call_duration_seconds Histogram function_name Call duration on SUCCESS events

The histogram is only observed when event.duration is set (i.e., on SUCCESS events), so it accurately tracks successful call latencies without polluting data with non-call events like retries or circuit opens.

Note

Requires the prometheus-client package. Install with pip install prometheus-client.

docs.title: Health Check
docs.text:
health_check() returns a summary of resilience state for all registered functions in a registry:

from pyresilience import ResilienceRegistry, health_check

registry = ResilienceRegistry()
# ... register configs and decorate functions ...

status = health_check(registry)

Returns a dict like:

{
    "payment-api": {
        "circuit_breaker": "closed",
        "in_flight": 3,
        "rate_limiter_available": True,
    },
    "inventory-service": {
        "circuit_breaker": "open",
        "in_flight": 0,
        "rate_limiter_available": True,
    },
}

Expose it from your health endpoint:

@app.get("/health/resilience")
def resilience_health():
    return health_check(registry)

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: pyresilience is designed to add minimal overhead to your function calls. Benchmarked on macOS (Apple Silicon) across Python 3.10 — 3.14; the 0.5.0 feature table below was measured on Windows with Python 3.14 and 3.15.

docs.title: Overhead
docs.text:
Measured with 100k calls per benchmark. These are real numbers, not estimates.

Pattern Mean Latency No decorator (baseline) 0.07μs Retry (happy path, no failures) 0.64μs Circuit breaker (closed state) 1.03μs Fallback (triggered) 0.69μs Bulkhead (acquire/release) 0.74μs Rate limiter (within limits) 0.89μs Cache (hit) 0.68μs All 7 patterns combined (cache hit) 0.67μs

For any real-world I/O operation (HTTP calls at ~50ms, DB queries at ~5ms), pyresilience's overhead is <0.02%.

docs.title: Happy Path (no failures, 100k calls)
docs.text: Library Mean vs pyresilience pyresilience 0.64μs 1.0x pybreaker 0.64μs 1.0x backoff 1.29μs 2.0x slower stamina 5.33μs 8.3x slower tenacity 6.64μs 10.4x slower

docs.title: Throughput (10k calls, 10 threads, ops/sec)
docs.text: Library ops/sec vs pyresilience pyresilience 223,934 1.0x tenacity 58,109 3.9x slower

docs.title: Async (50k calls)
docs.text: Library Mean vs pyresilience pyresilience 0.82μs 1.0x tenacity 11.83μs 14.4x slower

docs.title: Memory (1,000 decorated functions)
docs.text: Library Memory pyresilience 1,224 KB tenacity 2,150 KB

docs.title: 0.5.0 Feature Overhead
docs.text:
Cost of one successful decorated call with the features added in 0.5.0, from benchmarks/bench_new_features.py. Measured on Windows 11 (x86-64) with Python 3.14.4 and 3.15.1, minimum of 7 alternating runs. This is a different machine than the tables above, so compare within this table only.

Configuration Python 3.14 Python 3.15 bare function (baseline) 0.03μs 0.02μs Rate limiter: plain (one token per call) 1.57μs 1.23μs Rate limiter: weighted cost 2.47μs 1.86μs Rate limiter: three limits at once 2.68μs 2.21μs Rate limiter: token reconcile + server feedback 4.73μs 3.74μs Rate limiter: shared through a backend (in-memory) 3.96μs 3.26μs Fallback: plain handler 1.19μs 0.93μs Fallback: alternatives + cooldown (primary healthy) 1.66μs 1.27μs Fallback: primary cooling down, alternative used 1.60μs 1.24μs Shared circuit breaker + retry budget 1.88μs 1.34μs Registry: state shared by sync and async (sync call) 2.27μs 1.77μs Registry: state shared by sync and async (async call) 2.99μs 2.36μs Timeout: per attempt (sync, worker thread) 21.11μs 21.34μs Timeout: per attempt + overall deadline (sync) 22.39μs 20.88μs Stream idle timeout (async, per item) 2.51μs 1.96μs

What the numbers say:

  • Weighted and multi-limit rate limiting costs about 0.6 to 1.1μs more than the plain limiter. The plain limiter is still used whenever the configuration needs nothing more.
  • Reconciliation and server feedback wrap the call to observe its result, which adds about 2μs.
  • Shared rate limits add one backend round trip per call. The figure above is for the in-memory backend; with Redis expect the network round trip (typically 0.2 to 1 ms).
  • Shared circuit breaker and retry budget cost nothing on the call path beyond two counters; the exchange with the backend runs in a background thread.
  • The overall deadline adds no measurable cost to a call with a timeout. Sync timeouts are dominated by the hop through a worker thread; async timeouts are not.
  • The stream idle timeout costs about 2 to 2.5μs per item for async streams (asyncio.wait_for per item). A sync stream hands every item from its reader thread to the caller, which cost about 15μs per item on this machine.

docs.title: Hot Path Check Against 0.4.1
docs.text:
benchmarks/bench_compare.py times the bench_overhead.py configurations against two source trees in short alternating rounds. Working tree against 0.4.1, Python 3.14, same machine, median of 25 rounds for each side:

Configuration 0.4.1 0.5.0 Change @resilient (default retry) 1.01μs 1.00μs -0.6% Retry only 1.26μs 1.26μs -0.4% Retry + ignore_on 1.26μs 1.27μs +0.8% Retry + delay_func 1.28μs 1.26μs -1.6% Retry + timeout (sync) 21.39μs 22.01μs +2.9% Retry + circuit breaker 1.81μs 1.82μs +0.1% All patterns (no cache) 23.74μs 23.81μs +0.3% Cache (hit) 2.37μs 2.36μs -0.1%

Every configuration is within 3% of 0.4.1, which is run-to-run noise. The table shows medians because the fastest round is not stable for the sync timeout rows, where every call hops through a worker thread. Features that are not configured cost nothing measurable.

docs.title: Python 3.15
docs.text: Python 3.15 is supported and tested in CI. On the same machine most benchmark configurations ran 18 to 29% faster than on Python 3.14 (retry + circuit breaker: 1.31μs against 1.72μs; weighted rate limiter: 1.86μs against 2.47μs). Sync timeouts do not improve: they are bound by the hop through a worker thread.

docs.title: uvloop
docs.text:
uvloop is a C-based event loop that's 2-4x faster than the default asyncio loop.

pip install pyresilience[fast]

from pyresilience import install_uvloop

install_uvloop()  # Sets uvloop as the default event loop policy

Note

uvloop is only available on Linux and macOS (not Windows). pyresilience gracefully handles this — install_uvloop() returns False on unsupported platforms.

Listener exceptions are logged as warnings (via logging.warning()) to prevent broken observability from being silently swallowed, while still protecting the application from listener failures.

docs.title: orjson
docs.text:
orjson is a Rust-based JSON library that's ~10x faster than stdlib json. It's automatically used by JsonEventLogger when available.

pip install pyresilience[fast]

No code changes needed — JsonEventLogger auto-detects orjson.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Check what's available at runtime:

from pyresilience import has_uvloop, has_orjson

print(f"uvloop: {has_uvloop()}")  # True/False
print(f"orjson: {has_orjson()}")  # True/False

docs.title: Cache Stampede Prevention
docs.text: When a popular cache key expires, many threads/coroutines may simultaneously attempt to recompute the value (thundering herd). pyresilience uses per-key locking with a double-check pattern: only one thread/coroutine computes per cache key while others wait for the result. This eliminates redundant work and protects downstream services from load spikes.

docs.title: Sync Timeout Thread Cancellation
docs.text: When a sync function exceeds its timeout, pyresilience uses ctypes.pythonapi.PyThreadState_SetAsyncExc for best-effort thread interruption on CPython. This raises an exception in the worker thread, allowing cleanup to occur. Note that blocking C extensions (e.g., socket.recv() without a timeout) cannot be interrupted by this mechanism. The original exception chain is preserved via from exc.

docs.title: Thread Safety
docs.text:
All pyresilience components are thread-safe:

  • CircuitBreaker: Uses threading.Lock for all state transitions — safe for free-threaded Python 3.13+
  • Bulkhead: Atomic counter with threading.Lock (non-waiting), threading.Semaphore (waiting)
  • RateLimiter: Uses threading.Lock (also the weighted limiter, whose single lock is shared by sync and async callers)
  • Fallback cooldown: Uses threading.Lock
  • Shared state: InMemoryBackend uses threading.Lock; backend increments must be atomic
  • ResultCache: Uses threading.Lock
  • Registry: Uses threading.Lock
  • MetricsCollector: Uses threading.Lock + contextvars for async-safe latency tracking. Latencies bounded to 10,000 entries.

You can safely share these across threads without external synchronization.

docs.title: Async Performance
docs.text:
For async code, pyresilience uses native asyncio primitives:

  • Timeout: asyncio.wait_for() (no threads)
  • Bulkhead: asyncio.Semaphore
  • Rate limiter: asyncio.sleep() for waiting
  • Retry delay: asyncio.sleep() (non-blocking)

docs.title: 1. Use presets for common patterns
docs.text:
Presets are tuned for typical use cases and avoid over-configuration:

@resilient(**http_policy())  # Tuned defaults
def call_api(): ...

docs.title: 2. Cache aggressively for read-heavy workloads
docs.text:
@resilient(cache=CacheConfig(max_size=1000, ttl=60.0))
def get_config(key: str) -> str: ...

docs.title: 3. Use bulkheads to protect connection pools
docs.text:
@resilient(bulkhead=BulkheadConfig(max_concurrent=pool_size))
def db_query(sql: str): ...

docs.title: 4. Keep listeners lightweight
docs.text:
Listeners run synchronously in the calling thread. Avoid heavy I/O in listeners:

# Good: append to list, increment counter
def fast_listener(event):
    metrics.append(event)

# Bad: HTTP call in listener
def slow_listener(event):
    requests.post("https://monitoring.example.com", json=event)  # Don't do this

docs.title: Presets
docs.text: Presets are opinionated default configurations for common integration patterns. Instead of tuning every parameter, pick a preset that matches your use case.

docs.title: http_policy()
docs.text:
Optimized for HTTP API calls — fast timeout, moderate retries, standard circuit breaker.

from pyresilience import resilient
from pyresilience.presets import http_policy

@resilient(**http_policy())
def call_api(url: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(url).json()
Parameter Default Why Timeout 10s APIs should respond quickly Max retries 3 Enough to handle transient failures Retry delay 0.5s Start fast, backoff exponentially Backoff factor 2.0 Standard exponential backoff Max delay 30s Don't wait too long between retries Circuit failure threshold 5 Open after 5 failures Circuit recovery 30s Check again after 30 seconds Jitter Yes Prevent thundering herd

Customizable:

@resilient(**http_policy(
    timeout_seconds=5.0,
    max_retries=5,
    circuit_failure_threshold=10,
    rate_limit=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=100, period=60.0),
    cache=CacheConfig(max_size=256, ttl=300.0),
))
def call_api(): ...

docs.title: db_policy()
docs.text:
Optimized for database calls — longer timeout, fewer retries, connection pool protection.

from pyresilience.presets import db_policy

@resilient(**db_policy())
def query_db(sql: str) -> list:
    return cursor.execute(sql).fetchall()
Parameter Default Why Timeout 30s Queries can be slow Max retries 2 Fewer retries to avoid connection pile-up Retry delay 1.0s Longer initial delay Backoff factor 1.5 Less aggressive than HTTP Max delay 10s Don't wait too long Circuit failure threshold 3 Trip faster — DB issues are serious Circuit recovery 60s Give the DB more time to recover Bulkhead 10 concurrent Protect connection pool

docs.title: queue_policy()
docs.text:
Optimized for message queue producers/consumers — more retries, higher failure tolerance.

from pyresilience.presets import queue_policy

@resilient(**queue_policy())
async def publish_message(msg: dict) -> None:
    await producer.send(msg)
Parameter Default Why Timeout 15s Moderate timeout Max retries 5 Messages should eventually be delivered Retry delay 2.0s Longer delay for queue recovery Backoff factor 2.0 Standard exponential Max delay 60s Allow long waits for queue recovery Circuit failure threshold 10 Higher tolerance — queues are bursty Circuit recovery 60s Standard recovery time

docs.title: strict_policy()
docs.text:
Fail-fast policy for latency-sensitive paths where slow is worse than failing.

from pyresilience.presets import strict_policy

@resilient(**strict_policy())
def cache_lookup(key: str) -> dict:
    return redis_client.get(key)
Parameter Default Why Timeout 5s Fail fast Max attempts 1 No retries (1 total attempt) Retry delay 0.1s Minimal delay Backoff factor 1.0 No backoff Max delay 0.5s Cap very low Circuit failure threshold 3 Trip quickly Circuit recovery 60s Standard recovery Jitter No Deterministic for debugging

docs.title: llm_policy()
docs.text:
Optimized for LLM and rate-limited HTTP APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Stripe, GitHub, ...) — retries on 429/5xx responses, honors the server's Retry-After header, and throttles client-side so you hit the rate limit less often in the first place.

from pyresilience import resilient, llm_policy

@resilient(**llm_policy())
def ask_model(prompt: str):
    return client.chat.completions.create(model="...", messages=[...])
Parameter Default Why Timeout 60s LLM responses can be slow Max attempts 4 Rate limits usually clear within a few retries Retry delay 1.0s Base for exponential backoff when no Retry-After is present Retry on status 429, 500, 502, 503, 504 Retries these response codes via retry_on_status() Retry-After handling On, capped at 60s retry_after_delay() parses the header; falls back to backoff Rate limiter 60 calls / 60s Client-side smoothing to avoid 429s proactively Circuit failure threshold 5 Stop hammering a failing provider Circuit recovery 30s Re-probe after a short cool-down tokens_per_minute off Optional token limit next to the call limit; needs token_cost or token_usage adaptive_rate_limit off Follow Retry-After and rate-limit headers reported by the server rate_limit_max_wait 0s How long a call waits for rate-limit capacity before it is rejected

Customizable:

@resilient(**llm_policy(
    max_calls=500, period=60.0,                  # paid-tier rate limits
    retry_on_status_codes=(429,),                # only retry rate limits
    ignore_on=(AuthError, QuotaExceededError),   # terminal errors: no retry, no circuit failure
    max_concurrent=8,                            # optional bulkhead
))
def ask_model(prompt: str): ...

Token limits and server feedback:

@resilient(**llm_policy(
    tokens_per_minute=90_000,
    token_cost=lambda prompt: len(prompt) // 4 + 256,          # reserved before the call
    token_usage=lambda response: response.usage.total_tokens,  # settled after the call
    adaptive_rate_limit=True,
    rate_limit_max_wait=10.0,
))
def ask_model(prompt: str): ...

With tokens_per_minute set, retries are charged against the limits as well, because every retry spends real tokens. See RateLimiter.

ignore_on propagates to both the retry and the circuit breaker configs — terminal client errors fail fast and don't trip the circuit. See HTTP & LLM Helpers for the underlying retry_on_status() / retry_after_delay() building blocks.

docs.title: Custom Presets
docs.text:
Create your own presets following the same pattern:

from pyresilience._types import RetryConfig, TimeoutConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig, RateLimiterConfig

def my_api_policy(**overrides):
    defaults = {
        "retry": RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, delay=0.5),
        "timeout": TimeoutConfig(seconds=15),
        "circuit_breaker": CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
        "rate_limiter": RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=50, period=1.0),
    }
    defaults.update(overrides)
    return defaults

docs.title: Registry
docs.text: The registry provides centralized management of named resilience configurations. Multiple functions decorated with the same registry name share the same circuit breaker, rate limiter, and other stateful components.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Without a registry, each @resilient() call creates its own independent circuit breaker:

# These have SEPARATE circuit breakers — one can be open while the other is closed
@resilient(circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5))
def charge_card(): ...

@resilient(circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5))
def refund_card(): ...

With a registry, they share state:

registry = ResilienceRegistry()
registry.register("payment-api", ResilienceConfig(
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
))

# These SHARE the same circuit breaker
@registry.decorator("payment-api")
def charge_card(): ...

@registry.decorator("payment-api")
def refund_card(): ...

# If charge_card trips the circuit, refund_card is also blocked

docs.title: Basic Registry
docs.text:
from pyresilience import ResilienceRegistry, ResilienceConfig, RetryConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig

registry = ResilienceRegistry()

# Register named configurations
registry.register("payment-api", ResilienceConfig(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30),
))

registry.register("inventory-api", ResilienceConfig(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=2),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=3, recovery_timeout=60),
))

# Decorate functions
@registry.decorator("payment-api")
async def charge_card(amount: float) -> dict:
    return await payment_client.charge(amount)

@registry.decorator("payment-api")
async def refund_card(amount: float) -> dict:
    return await payment_client.refund(amount)

@registry.decorator("inventory-api")
async def check_stock(item_id: str) -> int:
    return await inventory_client.get_stock(item_id)

docs.title: Default Configuration
docs.text:
Set a default config for unregistered names:

registry = ResilienceRegistry()
registry.set_default(ResilienceConfig(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=2),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=10),
))

# Uses the default config since "analytics-api" isn't registered
@registry.decorator("analytics-api")
def track_event(event: dict) -> None:
    analytics_client.track(event)

docs.title: Querying the Registry
docs.text:
# Get a specific config
config = registry.get("payment-api")

# Get config with fallback to default
config = registry.get_or_default("unknown-api")

# List all registered names
names = registry.names  # ["payment-api", "inventory-api"]

# Remove a config
registry.unregister("payment-api")

# Clear everything
registry.clear()

docs.title: Dynamic Registration
docs.text:
Register configs at application startup:

# config.py
from pyresilience import ResilienceRegistry, ResilienceConfig, RetryConfig, CircuitBreakerConfig

registry = ResilienceRegistry()

def configure_resilience():
    """Call this at application startup."""
    registry.register("payment-api", ResilienceConfig(
        retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
        circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    ))
    registry.register("user-api", ResilienceConfig(
        retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=2),
        timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=5),
    ))

# services.py
from config import registry

@registry.decorator("payment-api")
async def charge(amount: float) -> dict: ...

@registry.decorator("user-api")
async def get_user(user_id: int) -> dict: ...

# main.py
from config import configure_resilience

configure_resilience()
# Now all decorated functions use the registered configs

docs.title: Shared State
docs.text:
The key benefit of the registry is shared state. Functions using the same registry name share:

  • Circuit breaker state — if one function trips the circuit, all functions under the same name are blocked
  • Rate limiter tokens — all functions share the same limits
  • Retry budget — all functions draw on the same budget
  • Fallback cooldown — a target that is cooling down is skipped by all functions
  • Bulkhead slots — concurrent calls across all functions of one call style count toward the same limit

This models real-world dependencies: if the payment API is down, all payment operations should fail fast — not just the one that discovered the failure.

docs.title: Sync and Async
docs.text:
The registry handles both sync and async functions transparently:

@registry.decorator("payment-api")
def sync_charge(amount: float) -> dict:
    return payment_client.charge(amount)

@registry.decorator("payment-api")
async def async_charge(amount: float) -> dict:
    return await payment_client.async_charge(amount)

Sync and async functions under one name share the circuit breaker, the rate limits, the retry budget and the fallback cooldown state: if sync_charge opens the circuit, async_charge is blocked too, and both count against the same rate limit.

Note

Bulkhead slots and cached results stay separate per call style. Sync functions share them with other sync functions, async functions with other async functions.

To share state between processes as well, add a SharedStateConfig to the registered config. See Shared State.

docs.title: Shared State
docs.text:
By default every process keeps its own circuit breaker, rate limits and retry budget. That is correct for one process and wrong for a fleet: with five replicas, a limit of 100 calls per minute becomes 500, and a circuit breaker with failure_threshold=5 lets 25 failures through before any replica opens.

SharedStateConfig stores that state in a backend so that all processes act as one.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import redis
from redis.backoff import NoBackoff
from redis.retry import Retry
from pyresilience import (
    resilient, CircuitBreakerConfig, RateLimiterConfig, RetryBudgetConfig,
    RetryConfig, SharedStateConfig,
)
from pyresilience.contrib.redis import RedisBackend

client = redis.Redis(
    host="localhost",
    port=6379,
    socket_connect_timeout=0.5,   # rate-limited calls wait for this client,
    socket_timeout=0.5,           # so keep its timeouts short
    retry=Retry(NoBackoff(), 0),  # and switch off its own retries
)
shared = SharedStateConfig(backend=RedisBackend(client), key="payment-api")

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=100, period=60.0),
    retry_budget=RetryBudgetConfig(max_retries=50, refill_rate=5.0),
    shared_state=shared,
)
def charge(amount: float) -> dict:
    return payment_client.charge(amount)

Every process that runs this code with the same backend and key now shares one rate limit, one circuit breaker and one retry budget.

pyresilience does not depend on a Redis library. RedisBackend takes the client you already use; any client with redis-py's synchronous API works.

docs.title: What Is Shared, and How
docs.text: Pattern Shared Mechanism Accuracy Rate limiter Yes Every call is counted in the backend (atomic increment of a fixed window) Acquisitions never exceed a window; corrections are conservative Circuit breaker Yes Background pass every sync_interval seconds Open state arrives within two passes: one publishes it, one adopts it Retry budget Yes Background pass every sync_interval seconds Converges on one budget; a burst shorter than a pass is not capped Fallback cooldown No In-process — Bulkhead No In-process — Cache No In-process —

docs.title: Rate limiter
docs.text:
Each acquisition increments a counter for the current window (period seconds long) in the backend. The increment is atomic, so all processes together cannot exceed the limit of a window. The local token bucket still applies first, so a single process stays within the limit on its own, also while the backend is down.

  • Weighted costs, several limits and reconciliation with the real cost all carry over to the shared counters.
  • One backend round trip per call (plus one per additional limit). For async functions the round trip runs in a worker thread, so the event loop is not blocked.
  • Shared windows are fixed windows aligned to the wall clock; the local limiter is a token bucket.
  • Fixed windows can pass up to twice the limit across a boundary: a full window at the end of one period and another at the start of the next. If the provider enforces a rolling window, set the limit with that in mind.
  • A correction after the call (actual_cost) goes to the window the call was counted in. If that window has already passed, unused units are not given back, because the later window never held them. Usage above the estimate is charged to the current window.
  • A pause from server feedback (Retry-After) applies to the process that received it. Other processes learn the same from their own responses.

docs.title: Circuit breaker
docs.text:
Every process keeps deciding locally, so a call never waits for the backend. A background pass exchanges:

  • The open state. When one instance opens, the others open within two passes at most (one publishes the state, one adopts it) and recover at the same moment.
  • The failure streak (consecutive-count mode). Failures of all instances add up, so failure_threshold=5 means five failures across the fleet. A success on any instance ends the shared streak. The streak is exchanged once per pass, so the exact order of failures and successes between instances inside one interval is not preserved.

Sliding-window breakers share only the open state: a failure rate is the same on every instance and needs no adding up.

Shared state means shared fate

An instance that cannot reach the dependency because of its own network problem will open the circuit for everyone. Use ignore_on for errors that say nothing about the dependency's health.

docs.title: Retry budget
docs.text: Each pass publishes the retries a process spent and debits the retries the others spent. Over time the fleet converges on one budget. Between two passes each process still spends what it believed it had, so a burst of retries that is shorter than sync_interval is limited by every process's own budget, not by the shared one. Use a short sync_interval when retry storms are the concern.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from pyresilience import SharedStateConfig

SharedStateConfig(
    backend=backend,      # where the state lives
    key="payment-api",    # name of the state in the backend
    sync_interval=1.0,    # seconds between background passes
    fail_open=True,       # behaviour of rate limiting while the backend is down
)
Parameter Type Default Description backend StateBackend required InMemoryBackend(), RedisBackend(client) or your own key str "" Everything using the same backend and key shares state. Defaults to the registry name, or to module.qualname of the function decorated with @resilient sync_interval float 1.0 Seconds between background passes for circuit breaker and retry budget. 0 starts no thread; call sync_now() yourself fail_open bool True While the backend cannot be reached: True keeps rate limiting on the local limit, False rejects calls

Set an explicit key:

  • when the default would differ between deployments of the same service, for example when the function lives in a module that is imported under different names;
  • for functions created inside a factory or closure, which would otherwise all share one default key;
  • with the FastAPI, Django and Flask integrations, which have no function path to derive a key from. Leaving it empty there raises ValueError.

docs.title: When the Backend Is Down
docs.text:
A backend failure never raises into your call.

Pattern fail_open=True (default) fail_open=False Rate limiter Calls proceed on this process's local limit Calls are rejected with RateLimitExceededError Circuit breaker Keeps working on local state Same Retry budget Keeps working on local state Same

The first failure of an outage is logged as a warning on the pyresilience logger, the following ones at debug level.

After a failed backend call, rate limiting leaves the backend alone for sync_interval seconds (at least one second) and answers at once according to fail_open. After a slow failure the pause is longer: ten times as long as the failed call took, up to 30 seconds, so that a client that is slow to give up cannot keep a caller waiting most of the time. When the pause is over, one call tries the backend again. While it is trying, the other calls keep being answered at once, so one call at a time waits for a backend that is down. If that call has not come back after 30 seconds, another one tries.

That one call still waits for the client to give up, and so does every call that was already talking to the backend when it went down. Give the client you pass to RedisBackend short timeouts (socket_connect_timeout, socket_timeout) and few or no retries of its own, as the Quick Start does: the client's defaults can add up to many seconds.

docs.title: With the Registry
docs.text:
Put shared_state in the registered config. The registry name becomes the key:

registry = ResilienceRegistry()
registry.register("payment-api", ResilienceConfig(
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=100, period=60.0),
    shared_state=SharedStateConfig(backend=RedisBackend(client)),
))

@registry.decorator("payment-api")
def charge(amount: float) -> dict: ...

Without a backend, a registry name already shares circuit breaker, rate limits, retry budget and fallback cooldown between the sync and async functions of one process. See Registry.

docs.title: InMemoryBackend
docs.text:
Keeps the state in process memory. It shares state between separate @resilient functions and registries of one process, and replaces a real backend in tests:

from pyresilience import InMemoryBackend, SharedStateConfig

backend = InMemoryBackend()
shared = SharedStateConfig(backend=backend, key="svc", sync_interval=0)

# ... exercise the functions ...
shared.sync_now()   # run one pass deterministically

docs.title: RedisBackend
docs.text:
from pyresilience.contrib.redis import RedisBackend

backend = RedisBackend(redis.Redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379/0"), prefix="myapp:")

It uses GET, SET with PX, INCRBYFLOAT, PEXPIRE and DEL. Keys are written with an expiry, so abandoned state cleans itself up. Increment and expiry travel in one pipeline (one round trip) when the client offers pipeline().

docs.title: Writing Your Own
docs.text:
A backend is any object with these four methods. incr must be atomic.

from typing import Optional

class MyBackend:
    def get(self, key: str) -> Optional[str]: ...
    def set(self, key: str, value: str, ttl: Optional[float] = None) -> None: ...
    def incr(self, key: str, amount: float, ttl: Optional[float] = None) -> float: ...
    def delete(self, key: str) -> None: ...

isinstance(MyBackend(), pyresilience.StateBackend) is True for any object with these methods.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
• Clocks. Shared timestamps use the wall clock. Clock skew between hosts shifts the shared recovery moment of a circuit breaker and the window boundaries of a rate limit by the skew. Keep hosts on NTP.
  • Manual control. reset(), force_open() and force_close() act on the local breaker. A reset also clears the shared record at the next pass; instances that already adopted the open state stay open until their recovery time.
  • Background thread. One daemon thread per SharedStateConfig runs the passes. It stops when nothing uses the config any more.
  • Forked workers. Threads do not survive fork(). A forked child (gunicorn with --preload, Celery's prefork pool, multiprocessing with the fork start method) starts its own background thread automatically, so functions decorated before the fork keep syncing. uWSGI forks its workers without running Python's fork hooks, so there the thread is not restarted and the workers do not sync: start uWSGI with py-call-osafterfork = true or lazy-apps = true. Also set enable-threads = true, as uWSGI's documentation requires for threads the application starts.
  • Latency. Only rate limiting adds a backend round trip to the call. Circuit breaker and retry budget cost nothing on the call path.

docs.title: Bulkhead
docs.text: The bulkhead pattern limits the number of concurrent executions to prevent resource exhaustion. Named after the compartments in a ship's hull that prevent a single breach from sinking the entire vessel.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
A bulkhead acts as a semaphore that limits how many calls can execute simultaneously:

                    Bulkhead (max_concurrent=3)
                    ┌──────────────────────────┐
Request 1 ────────> │  Slot 1: [executing]     │
Request 2 ────────> │  Slot 2: [executing]     │
Request 3 ────────> │  Slot 3: [executing]     │
                    └──────────────────────────┘
Request 4 ────────> REJECTED (BulkheadFullError)

This prevents a single slow dependency from consuming all available threads/connections in your application.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from pyresilience import BulkheadConfig

config = BulkheadConfig(
    max_concurrent=10,  # Allow up to 10 concurrent executions
    max_wait=0.0,       # Fail immediately if no slot available (0 = no waiting)
)
Parameter Type Default Description max_concurrent int 10 Maximum number of concurrent executions max_wait float 0.0 Maximum seconds to wait for a slot. 0 means fail immediately.

docs.title: Basic Bulkhead
docs.text:
from pyresilience import resilient, BulkheadConfig

@resilient(bulkhead=BulkheadConfig(max_concurrent=5))
def query_database(sql: str) -> list:
    return cursor.execute(sql).fetchall()

If more than 5 calls are in progress, new calls raise BulkheadFullError.

docs.title: With Waiting
docs.text:
Allow callers to wait briefly for a slot:

@resilient(bulkhead=BulkheadConfig(max_concurrent=10, max_wait=5.0))
def call_api() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

Callers wait up to 5 seconds for a slot. If no slot opens, BulkheadFullError is raised.

docs.title: With Fallback
docs.text:
Return a degraded response instead of raising:

from pyresilience import resilient, BulkheadConfig, FallbackConfig, BulkheadFullError

@resilient(
    bulkhead=BulkheadConfig(max_concurrent=10),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(
        handler=lambda e: {"status": "busy", "retry_after": 5},
        fallback_on=(BulkheadFullError,),
    ),
)
def get_data() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com/data").json()

docs.title: Protecting Database Connection Pools
docs.text:
@resilient(bulkhead=BulkheadConfig(max_concurrent=20, max_wait=3.0))
def db_query(sql: str) -> list:
    with connection_pool.get_connection() as conn:
        return conn.execute(sql).fetchall()

docs.title: Async Loop Safety
docs.text:
AsyncBulkhead automatically detects event loop changes and recreates its internal semaphore. This makes it safe to use across multiple asyncio.run() calls without manual cleanup:

@resilient(bulkhead=BulkheadConfig(max_concurrent=5))
async def my_func():
    return await some_async_call()

asyncio.run(my_func())  # First loop — semaphore created
asyncio.run(my_func())  # New loop detected — semaphore recreated automatically

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Event When EventType.BULKHEAD_REJECTED A call was rejected because the bulkhead is full

docs.title: Exception
docs.text:
from pyresilience import BulkheadFullError

try:
    result = my_function()
except BulkheadFullError:
    # No concurrent slots available
    return fallback_response()

docs.title: Cache
docs.text: The cache pattern stores successful function results and returns them on subsequent calls with the same arguments, avoiding redundant calls to slow backends.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The cache sits at the outermost layer of the execution pipeline. Before any other resilience pattern is applied, the cache is checked:

call(args) ──> Cache HIT? ──yes──> Return cached result
                   |
                   no
                   |
                   v
           Execute with all other patterns
                   |
                   v
           Store result in cache

The cache uses:

  • LRU eviction — Least Recently Used entries are evicted when the cache reaches max_size
  • TTL expiration — Entries expire after ttl seconds

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from pyresilience import CacheConfig

config = CacheConfig(
    max_size=256,   # Maximum number of cached entries
    ttl=300.0,      # Time-to-live: 5 minutes
)
Parameter Type Default Description max_size int 256 Maximum number of cached entries. Oldest entries are evicted (LRU). ttl float 300.0 Time-to-live in seconds. 0 means entries never expire.

docs.title: Basic Caching
docs.text:
from pyresilience import resilient, CacheConfig

@resilient(cache=CacheConfig(max_size=100, ttl=60.0))
def get_user(user_id: int) -> dict:
    return requests.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}").json()

get_user(42)  # Calls API
get_user(42)  # Returns cached result (API not called)
get_user(99)  # Different args, calls API

docs.title: Cache Key Generation
docs.text:
Cache keys are generated from function arguments automatically:

@resilient(cache=CacheConfig())
def search(query: str, page: int = 1) -> list:
    return api.search(query, page)

search("python", page=1)  # Cached separately from:
search("python", page=2)  # Different key due to different args

docs.title: No Expiration
docs.text:
For data that rarely changes:

@resilient(cache=CacheConfig(max_size=1000, ttl=0))
def get_config(key: str) -> str:
    return config_service.get(key)

With ttl=0, entries never expire (only evicted by LRU when max_size is reached).

docs.title: Short TTL for Real-Time Data
docs.text:
@resilient(cache=CacheConfig(max_size=50, ttl=5.0))
def get_stock_price(symbol: str) -> float:
    return market_api.get_price(symbol)

docs.title: Cache + Retry + Circuit Breaker
docs.text:
Cache prevents redundant calls even when the service is healthy. If the cache misses, other patterns protect the call:

@resilient(
    cache=CacheConfig(max_size=256, ttl=300.0),
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=10),
)
def get_product(product_id: int) -> dict:
    return requests.get(f"https://api.example.com/products/{product_id}").json()

docs.title: Async Caching
docs.text:
@resilient(cache=CacheConfig(max_size=100, ttl=60.0))
async def async_get_user(user_id: int) -> dict:
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}") as resp:
            return await resp.json()

docs.title: Stampede Prevention
docs.text:
When a cache key expires under high concurrency, many threads or coroutines may simultaneously attempt to recompute the value (thundering herd). pyresilience prevents this with per-key locking and a double-check pattern: only one thread/coroutine computes per cache key while others wait for the result. This eliminates redundant work and protects downstream services from load spikes.

No configuration is needed — stampede prevention is always active.

docs.title: Events
Direct Usage
docs.text:
Use the cache directly without the decorator:

from pyresilience import ResultCache, CacheConfig

cache = ResultCache(CacheConfig(max_size=100, ttl=60.0))

# Store and retrieve
key = ResultCache.make_key("user", 42)
