cache.put(key, {"name": "Alice"})
result = cache.get(key)  # {"name": "Alice"}

# Invalidate
cache.invalidate(key)

# Statistics
print(cache.stats)
# {'hits': 1, 'misses': 0, 'hit_rate': 1.0, 'size': 0, 'max_size': 100}

# Clear all
cache.clear()

docs.title: Cache Statistics
docs.text:
Monitor cache effectiveness:

cache = ResultCache(CacheConfig(max_size=100, ttl=60.0))

# After some usage:
stats = cache.stats
print(f"Hit rate: {stats['hit_rate']:.1%}")  # "Hit rate: 85.0%"
print(f"Size: {stats['size']}/{stats['max_size']}")  # "Size: 42/100"

docs.title: CircuitBreaker
docs.text: The circuit breaker pattern prevents an application from repeatedly trying to execute an operation that is likely to fail. It allows the system to recover by temporarily blocking calls to a failing service.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The circuit breaker has three states:

CLOSED ──(failures >= threshold)──> OPEN
  ^                                    |
  |                            (recovery_timeout)
  |                                    |
  └──(successes >= threshold)── HALF_OPEN
State Behavior CLOSED Normal operation. Calls pass through. Failures are counted. OPEN All calls are immediately rejected with CircuitOpenError. No calls reach the protected function. HALF_OPEN A limited number of calls are allowed through to test if the service has recovered.

docs.title: State Transitions
docs.text:
• CLOSED -> OPEN: When consecutive failures reach failure_threshold, or failure rate exceeds failure_rate_threshold within a sliding window
  • OPEN -> HALF_OPEN: After recovery_timeout seconds have elapsed
  • HALF_OPEN -> CLOSED: When success_threshold consecutive successes occur
  • HALF_OPEN -> OPEN: On any failure during the half-open period

docs.title: Basic (consecutive count)
docs.text:
from pyresilience import CircuitBreakerConfig

config = CircuitBreakerConfig(
    failure_threshold=5,      # Open after 5 consecutive failures
    recovery_timeout=30.0,    # Wait 30s before trying again
    success_threshold=2,      # Need 2 successes in half-open to close
    error_types=(Exception,), # Which exceptions count as failures
)

docs.title: Sliding Window (failure rate %)
docs.text:
config = CircuitBreakerConfig(
    sliding_window_size=100,        # Track last 100 calls
    failure_rate_threshold=0.5,     # Open at 50% failure rate
    minimum_calls=10,               # Need at least 10 calls before evaluating
    recovery_timeout=30.0,
)

docs.title: Slow Call Detection
docs.text:
config = CircuitBreakerConfig(
    sliding_window_size=100,
    failure_rate_threshold=0.5,
    slow_call_duration=2.0,         # Calls > 2s are "slow"
    slow_call_rate_threshold=0.8,   # Open if 80% of calls are slow
)
Parameter Type Default Description failure_threshold int 5 Consecutive failures before the circuit opens (used when sliding_window_size=0) recovery_timeout float 30.0 Seconds to wait in OPEN before transitioning to HALF_OPEN success_threshold int 2 Consecutive successes in HALF_OPEN needed to close the circuit error_types Sequence[Type] (Exception,) Exception types that count as failures sliding_window_size int 0 Size of sliding window (0 = use consecutive count mode) failure_rate_threshold float 0.5 Failure rate (0.0–1.0) to trip the circuit in sliding window mode minimum_calls int 0 Minimum calls in window before evaluating thresholds slow_call_duration float 0.0 Duration in seconds above which a call is considered "slow" (0 = disabled) slow_call_rate_threshold float 1.0 Slow call rate (0.0–1.0) to trip the circuit ignore_on Sequence[Type] () Exception types that never count as failures; takes precedence over error_types

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from pyresilience import resilient, CircuitBreakerConfig

@resilient(circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(
    failure_threshold=5,
    recovery_timeout=30.0,
))
def call_payment_service(amount: float) -> dict:
    return requests.post("/charge", json={"amount": amount}).json()

docs.title: With Specific Error Types
docs.text:
Only count certain exceptions as failures:

import requests

@resilient(circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(
    failure_threshold=3,
    error_types=(requests.ConnectionError, requests.Timeout),
))
def call_api() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

ValueError or json.JSONDecodeError won't trip the circuit — only connection and timeout errors will.

docs.title: Ignoring Exceptions (ignore_on)
docs.text:
The inverse of error_types: list exceptions that must never count as circuit failures, even when they match error_types. Useful for client-side errors (bad input, auth failures, quota exhaustion) that say nothing about the downstream service's health:

@resilient(circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(
    failure_threshold=5,
    error_types=(Exception,),                 # count everything...
    ignore_on=(AuthError, ValidationError),   # ...except terminal client errors
))
def call_api() -> dict:
    return client.fetch()

Ignored exceptions still propagate to the caller — they just don't move the circuit toward OPEN. Pair with RetryConfig.ignore_on (see Retry) to also skip retries for the same types.

docs.title: With Fallback
docs.text:
Provide a fallback when the circuit is open:

from pyresilience import resilient, CircuitBreakerConfig, FallbackConfig

@resilient(
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(handler=lambda e: {"status": "degraded"}),
)
def get_status() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com/status").json()

When the circuit is open, instead of raising RuntimeError, the fallback value is returned.

docs.title: Async Usage
docs.text:
@resilient(circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5))
async def async_call() -> dict:
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get("https://api.example.com") as resp:
            return await resp.json()

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Access real-time circuit breaker metrics via the .metrics property:

from pyresilience._circuit_breaker import CircuitBreaker

cb = CircuitBreaker(CircuitBreakerConfig(
    sliding_window_size=100,
    failure_rate_threshold=0.5,
))

# After some calls...
print(cb.metrics)
# {"failure_rate": 0.15, "slow_call_rate": 0.0, "total_calls": 47, "state": "closed"}

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
The circuit breaker emits these events:

Event When EventType.CIRCUIT_OPEN Circuit transitions to OPEN (or a call is rejected while OPEN) EventType.CIRCUIT_HALF_OPEN Circuit transitions to HALF_OPEN EventType.CIRCUIT_CLOSED Circuit transitions back to CLOSED EventType.SLOW_CALL A call exceeded slow_call_duration 
from pyresilience import resilient, CircuitBreakerConfig, EventType

def on_event(event):
    if event.event_type == EventType.CIRCUIT_OPEN:
        alert_ops_team(f"Circuit opened for {event.function_name}")

@resilient(
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    listeners=[on_event],
)
def critical_service():
    ...

docs.title: Manual Control
docs.text:
For operational needs (maintenance windows, graceful degradation, testing), you can manually control circuit breaker state:

from pyresilience import CircuitBreaker, CircuitBreakerConfig

cb = CircuitBreaker(CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5))

# Force the circuit open (reject all calls)
cb.force_open()

# Force the circuit closed (allow all calls, reset counters)
cb.force_close()

# Reset to initial state (CLOSED with zeroed counters)
cb.reset()
Method Effect reset() Returns to CLOSED state, resets all failure/success counters force_open() Immediately transitions to OPEN, rejecting all calls force_close() Immediately transitions to CLOSED, resetting counters

These methods are thread-safe and can be called from any thread.

docs.title: Direct Usage
docs.text:
You can also use CircuitBreaker directly without the decorator:

from pyresilience import CircuitBreaker, CircuitBreakerConfig

cb = CircuitBreaker(CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=3))

if cb.allow_request():
    try:
        result = do_something()
        cb.record_success()
    except Exception:
        cb.record_failure()
        raise

# Check state
print(cb.state)  # CircuitState.CLOSED

docs.title: Fallback
docs.text: The fallback pattern decides what a caller gets when the protected call cannot succeed: a default value, the answer of another provider, or the original error.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
A failing call walks down a chain until something produces a value:

call fails (retries exhausted, circuit open, rate limited, bulkhead full, deadline spent)
     |
     v
 [alternatives]  tried in order with the original arguments ── first success ──> return
     |
     all failed or none configured
     |
     v
 [handler]  static value or fn(exc) ──────────────────────────────────────────> return
     |
     none configured
     |
     v
 raise the last error

With a cooldown, a target that keeps failing is skipped for a while, so callers stop paying for a provider that is known to be down:

cooldown=30, cooldown_threshold=1

Call 1:  primary fails ──> backup answers        (primary starts cooling down)
Call 2:  primary skipped ─> backup answers        (no time lost on the primary)
...
30s later: primary is tried again

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from pyresilience import FallbackConfig

config = FallbackConfig(
    handler=None,                 # Static value, fn(exc), or async fn(exc)
    fallback_on=(Exception,),     # Errors that start the chain
    alternatives=(),              # Callables tried with the original arguments
    cooldown=0.0,                 # Seconds a failing target is skipped (0 = off)
    cooldown_threshold=1,         # Consecutive failures that start a cooldown
)
Parameter Type Default Description handler Callable or any value None Last resort: a static value, fn(exc), or an async fn(exc) for async functions fallback_on Sequence[Type[BaseException]] (Exception,) Errors that start the fallback chain. Cleared to () when there is no handler and no alternative alternatives Sequence[Callable] () Callables tried in order with the original *args, **kwargs. The first success supplies the result cooldown float 0.0 Seconds a target is skipped after cooldown_threshold consecutive failures. 0 disables cooldown cooldown_threshold int 1 Consecutive failures that start a cooldown

Rejections raised by pyresilience itself (CircuitOpenError, RateLimitExceededError, BulkheadFullError) always start the chain, whatever fallback_on says. Errors listed in RetryConfig.ignore_on never do: they are raised immediately.

docs.title: Static Value or Handler
docs.text:
from pyresilience import resilient, FallbackConfig

@resilient(fallback=FallbackConfig(handler={"items": [], "stale": True}))
def list_items() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com/items").json()

@resilient(fallback=FallbackConfig(handler=lambda exc: {"error": str(exc)}))
def get_profile(user_id: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}").json()

docs.title: Alternatives: Another Provider With the Same Arguments
docs.text:
An alternative receives exactly what the decorated function received, so it can run the same request somewhere else:

from pyresilience import resilient, FallbackConfig, RetryConfig

def ask_backup_model(prompt: str, *, max_tokens: int = 256) -> str:
    return backup_client.complete(prompt, max_tokens=max_tokens)

def ask_small_model(prompt: str, *, max_tokens: int = 256) -> str:
    return small_client.complete(prompt, max_tokens=max_tokens)

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=2),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(
        alternatives=[ask_backup_model, ask_small_model],
        handler="Sorry, no model is available right now.",
    ),
)
def ask(prompt: str, *, max_tokens: int = 256) -> str:
    return primary_client.complete(prompt, max_tokens=max_tokens)

ask("hello", max_tokens=100) retries the primary twice, then calls ask_backup_model("hello", max_tokens=100), then ask_small_model(...), and finally returns the handler value.

An alternative can be decorated with @resilient itself, which gives it its own retry, timeout or circuit breaker.

docs.title: Cooldown: Stop Calling a Provider That Is Down
docs.text:
@resilient(
    fallback=FallbackConfig(
        alternatives=[ask_backup_model],
        cooldown=30.0,            # skip a failing target for 30 seconds
        cooldown_threshold=3,     # after 3 failures in a row
    ),
)
def ask(prompt: str) -> str:
    return primary_client.complete(prompt)
  • Each target (the decorated function and every alternative) has its own failure streak and cooldown.
  • A success resets the streak. When a cooldown ends, the streak starts again from zero.
  • While the decorated function cools down, calls go straight to the alternatives and the handler. The handler then receives the error that started the cooldown.
  • A cooldown never fails a call by itself. If every alternative is cooling down too and there is no handler, the decorated function is called anyway.

Cooldown also works with a handler alone:

@resilient(fallback=FallbackConfig(handler=load_cached_answer, cooldown=10.0))
def fetch_live(key: str) -> dict: ...

docs.title: Async
docs.text:
Use async alternatives and handlers with async functions (sync ones are accepted too). A sync function needs sync alternatives: an alternative that returns an awaitable raises TypeError.

async def ask_backup_model(prompt: str) -> str:
    return await backup_client.complete(prompt)

@resilient(fallback=FallbackConfig(alternatives=[ask_backup_model], cooldown=30.0))
async def ask(prompt: str) -> str:
    return await primary_client.complete(prompt)

docs.title: Cooldown or Circuit Breaker?
docs.text:
Cooldown Circuit breaker Scope One target of the fallback chain The whole decorated call While active Target is skipped, the chain continues Call is rejected with CircuitOpenError (the fallback chain still runs) Recovery Target is tried again after the cooldown Half-open probes, success threshold Use when You have somewhere else to send the call You want to stop calling a dependency and observe its recovery

They combine: an open circuit on the primary routes calls to the alternatives.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event When EventType.FALLBACK_USED An alternative or the handler supplied the result. detail is "alternative <name>" for alternatives EventType.COOLDOWN A target entered cooldown. detail is "<name> cooling down for <seconds>s"

With alternatives or a cooldown configured, a failing call emits FAILURE for the decorated function before FALLBACK_USED.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A stream that already started is not covered: alternatives run only when the call itself fails. Combine with TimeoutConfig.stream_idle_seconds to bound a stalled stream.
  • Results of alternatives are not written to the result cache. Cached results of the decorated function are still served while it cools down.
  • Alternatives run outside the timeout and the overall deadline of the decorated function. Decorate an alternative with @resilient(timeout=...) to bound it.
  • Local rejections (rate limit, bulkhead, open circuit) count toward the failure streak like errors of the function do. With cooldown_threshold=1, one rejected call starts a cooldown.
  • Cooldown state lives in the process. Under a registry name it is shared by sync and async functions.

docs.title: RateLimiter
docs.text: The rate limiter pattern controls the rate of calls to a function using a token bucket algorithm. Unlike the bulkhead (which limits concurrent calls), the rate limiter limits calls per time period.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The rate limiter uses a token bucket algorithm:

  • The bucket holds a maximum number of tokens (equal to max_calls)
  • Each call consumes one token
  • Tokens are refilled continuously at a rate of max_calls / period
  • If no tokens are available, the call is either rejected or waits
Token Bucket (max_calls=5, period=1.0)

Time 0.0s: [*] [*] [*] [*] [*]  (5 tokens)
Call 1:     [*] [*] [*] [*] [ ]  (4 tokens)
Call 2:     [*] [*] [*] [ ] [ ]  (3 tokens)
Call 3:     [*] [*] [ ] [ ] [ ]  (2 tokens)
Call 4:     [*] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]  (1 token)
Call 5:     [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]  (0 tokens)
Call 6:     REJECTED! (or waits for refill)

Time 0.2s: [*] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]  (1 token refilled)
Call 6:     [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]  (succeeds now)

docs.title: Rate Limiter vs Bulkhead
docs.text: Rate Limiter Bulkhead Limits Calls per time window Concurrent calls Use case API rate limits, throttling Connection pool protection Example 100 requests/minute 10 concurrent requests Algorithm Token bucket Semaphore

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from pyresilience import RateLimiterConfig

config = RateLimiterConfig(
    max_calls=10,    # 10 calls per period
    period=1.0,      # Per 1 second
    max_wait=0.0,    # Reject immediately if no tokens (0 = no waiting)
)
Parameter Type Default Description max_calls int 10 Maximum number of calls allowed per period period float 1.0 Time period in seconds max_wait float 0.0 Maximum seconds to wait for a token. 0 means reject immediately. cost Callable[..., float] None Receives the call's arguments and returns how many units of the primary limit the call consumes. Default: 1 per call actual_cost Callable[[Any], Optional[float]] None Receives the call's result and returns the units really consumed limits Sequence[RateLimit] () Additional limits enforced together with the primary one feedback Callable[[Any], Optional[RateLimitFeedback]] None Reads what the server reported about its limits from each attempt's result or exception charge_retries bool False Debit every retry attempt against the limits

The primary limit (max_calls per period) is named "calls". Each additional limit is a RateLimit:

Parameter Type Default Description max_units float required Units allowed per period (calls, tokens, bytes, ...) period float required Time period in seconds name str "limit<N>" Name used in events, errors and server feedback cost Callable[..., float] None Units a call consumes, computed from its arguments. Default: 1 per call actual_cost Callable[[Any], Optional[float]] None Units really consumed, computed from the result

docs.title: Basic Rate Limiting
docs.text:
from pyresilience import resilient, RateLimiterConfig

# Allow 10 requests per second
@resilient(rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=10, period=1.0))
def call_api(endpoint: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(endpoint).json()

docs.title: With Waiting
docs.text:
Allow callers to wait for a token instead of immediate rejection:

# 100 calls per minute, wait up to 5 seconds for a token
@resilient(rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(
    max_calls=100,
    period=60.0,
    max_wait=5.0,
))
def call_api() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

docs.title: Async Rate Limiting
docs.text:
@resilient(rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=50, period=1.0))
async def async_call() -> dict:
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get("https://api.example.com") as resp:
            return await resp.json()

docs.title: With Fallback
docs.text:
Return a queued/deferred response instead of rejecting:

from pyresilience import (
    resilient, RateLimiterConfig, FallbackConfig, RateLimitExceededError
)

@resilient(
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=10, period=1.0),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(
        handler=lambda e: {"status": "rate_limited", "retry_after": 1},
        fallback_on=(RateLimitExceededError,),
    ),
)
def call_api() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

docs.title: Combined with Circuit Breaker
docs.text:
@resilient(
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=100, period=60.0),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5),
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
)
def robust_call() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

docs.title: Several Limits at Once
docs.text:
A call proceeds only when every limit has capacity. When one limit rejects it, nothing is consumed from the others.

from pyresilience import resilient, RateLimit, RateLimiterConfig

# 10 calls per second AND 1,000 calls per day
@resilient(rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(
    max_calls=10,
    period=1.0,
    limits=[RateLimit(max_units=1000, period=86400.0, name="daily")],
))
def call_api() -> dict: ...

docs.title: Weighted Calls
docs.text:
Not every call costs the same. cost receives the call's arguments and returns its weight:

# A batch of 50 items uses 50 units of a 500-items-per-minute limit
@resilient(rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(
    max_calls=500,
    period=60.0,
    cost=lambda items: len(items),
))
def send_batch(items: list) -> None: ...

A call whose cost is larger than a limit's whole capacity can never pass and is rejected immediately, without waiting.

Waiting callers are not queued. With max_wait, a call with a large cost can be overtaken by smaller calls that keep taking the capacity it is waiting for, and is rejected when its wait runs out.

docs.title: Token Limits for LLM APIs
docs.text:
LLM providers limit requests per minute and tokens per minute. Reserve an estimate before the call and settle the difference afterwards:

@resilient(rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(
    max_calls=60,               # requests per minute
    period=60.0,
    max_wait=10.0,
    limits=[RateLimit(
        max_units=90_000,       # tokens per minute
        period=60.0,
        name="tokens",
        cost=lambda prompt, **kw: len(prompt) // 4 + kw.get("max_tokens", 256),
        actual_cost=lambda response: response.usage.total_tokens,
    )],
))
def complete(prompt: str, *, max_tokens: int = 256):
    return client.responses.create(model="...", input=prompt, max_output_tokens=max_tokens)
  • cost runs before the call and reserves the estimate.
  • actual_cost runs after a successful call. Unused tokens are given back; extra tokens are charged, which can put the limit into debt and delay later calls.
  • A failed call keeps its estimate charged.
  • With retries, the call has one reservation. It stays open across failed attempts and is settled by the first attempt that reports its usage; a later attempt that reports usage is debited what it used.
  • An exception raised by a cost function propagates to the caller.

docs.title: Following the Server
docs.text:
The server knows its limits better than any client-side estimate. A feedback function reads each attempt's response (or the response attached to a raised exception) and reports it back to the limiter:

from pyresilience import RateLimiterConfig, RateLimit
from pyresilience.contrib.http import rate_limit_feedback

RateLimiterConfig(
    max_calls=60,
    period=60.0,
    limits=[RateLimit(90_000, 60.0, name="tokens", cost=estimate_tokens)],
    feedback=rate_limit_feedback(),
)

rate_limit_feedback() understands Retry-After, OpenAI-style x-ratelimit-*, Anthropic-style anthropic-ratelimit-*, plain x-ratelimit-remaining / x-ratelimit-reset and the IETF RateLimit-* headers. See HTTP & LLM Helpers.

What the limiter does with the report:

Server says Limiter does Retry-After: 20 Pauses: no call is sent for 20 seconds. Callers wait if max_wait allows, else they are rejected 3 requests remaining Lowers the local "calls" level to 3 when it was higher 0 tokens remaining, resets in 12s Pauses for 12 seconds

A level is only ever lowered by feedback, never raised. You can write your own function returning a RateLimitFeedback(retry_after=..., remaining={...}).

rate_limit_feedback() reads the headers from result.headers, or from exc.response.headers for a raised error. Parsed result objects of LLM SDKs usually carry no headers, so with those the limiter only learns from errors unless the function returns the SDK's raw response.

docs.title: Charging Retries
docs.text:
By default capacity is taken once per call, and retries are free. With charge_retries=True each retry attempt is debited as well, without waiting, so a burst of retries slows down the calls that follow:

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=4),
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=60, period=60.0, charge_retries=True),
)
def call_api() -> dict: ...

docs.title: Sharing Limits Between Processes
docs.text: With several replicas, each process has its own bucket and the real rate is multiplied by the replica count. SharedStateConfig counts every call in a shared backend so the limit holds for the whole fleet. See Shared State.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event When EventType.RATE_LIMITED A call was rejected because the rate limit was exceeded

When the configuration uses cost, limits, feedback or charge_retries, the event's detail and the RateLimitExceededError message name the limit that rejected the call, for example limit 'tokens' exceeded, or server feedback while the limiter is paused.

docs.title: Exception
docs.text:
from pyresilience import RateLimitExceededError

try:
    result = my_function()
except RateLimitExceededError:
    # Rate limit exceeded, try again later
    time.sleep(1)

docs.title: Direct Usage
docs.text:
Use the rate limiter without the decorator:

from pyresilience import RateLimiter, RateLimiterConfig

rl = RateLimiter(RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=10, period=1.0))

if rl.acquire():
    result = do_something()
else:
    print("Rate limit exceeded")

# Reset to full capacity
rl.reset()

docs.title: Retry
docs.text: The retry pattern automatically retries a failed operation with configurable delays, backoff strategies, and jitter. This handles transient failures like network blips and temporary service unavailability.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
When a call fails with a retryable exception, the retry mechanism:

  1. Waits for a calculated delay
  2. Retries the operation
  3. Repeats until success or max attempts are exhausted

The delay between retries grows using exponential backoff:

attempt 1: delay = 1.0s
attempt 2: delay = 1.0 * 2.0 = 2.0s
attempt 3: delay = 2.0 * 2.0 = 4.0s  (capped at max_delay)

Jitter adds randomness to prevent the thundering herd problem — when many clients retry simultaneously after an outage.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from pyresilience import RetryConfig

config = RetryConfig(
    max_attempts=3,           # 3 total attempts (1 initial + 2 retries)
    delay=1.0,                # 1 second initial delay
    backoff_factor=2.0,       # Double the delay each retry
    max_delay=60.0,           # Never wait more than 60 seconds
    jitter=True,              # Add randomized jitter
    retry_on=(Exception,),    # Which exceptions to retry
)
Parameter Type Default Description max_attempts int 3 Total number of attempts (including the first call) delay float 1.0 Initial delay between retries in seconds backoff_factor float 2.0 Multiplier applied to delay after each retry max_delay float 60.0 Maximum delay between retries in seconds jitter bool True Add random jitter to delay (10% floor to 1.0x of calculated delay — never produces zero-delay) retry_on Sequence[Type] (Exception,) Exception types that trigger a retry retry_on_result Callable[[Any], bool] None Predicate to retry based on return value ignore_on Sequence[Type] () Exception types that are never retried; takes precedence over retry_on delay_func Callable[[int, Any], Optional[float]] None Dynamic per-attempt delay computed from the triggering exception or result

docs.title: Basic Retry
docs.text:
from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, delay=1.0))
def fetch_data():
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com/data").json()

docs.title: Custom Exception Types
docs.text:
Only retry on specific exceptions:

import requests

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(
    max_attempts=5,
    retry_on=(requests.ConnectionError, requests.Timeout),
))
def call_api() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

A ValueError will not be retried — it will propagate immediately.

docs.title: Aggressive Retry for Queues
docs.text:
@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(
    max_attempts=10,
    delay=2.0,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    max_delay=120.0,
    jitter=True,
))
async def publish_message(msg: dict) -> None:
    await producer.send(msg)

docs.title: No Backoff (Fixed Delay)
docs.text:
@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(
    max_attempts=3,
    delay=0.5,
    backoff_factor=1.0,  # No exponential increase
    jitter=False,
))
def simple_retry():
    return do_something()

docs.title: Retry on Result
docs.text:
Retry based on return values instead of (or in addition to) exceptions:

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(
    max_attempts=5,
    delay=1.0,
    retry_on_result=lambda r: r.get("status") == 429,  # Retry on rate limit
))
def call_api() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

The predicate receives the return value. If it returns True, the call is retried. On the last attempt, the result is returned regardless of the predicate.

# Retry until a non-empty result
@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(
    max_attempts=3,
    delay=0.5,
    retry_on_result=lambda r: r is None or len(r) == 0,
))
def poll_queue() -> list:
    return queue.receive_messages()

docs.title: Never Retry Certain Exceptions (ignore_on)
docs.text:
Some failures are terminal — invalid credentials, exhausted quotas, malformed requests. Retrying them wastes time and can mask the real bug. ignore_on lists exception types that are re-raised immediately, even when they also match retry_on:

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(
    max_attempts=5,
    retry_on=(Exception,),            # retry everything...
    ignore_on=(AuthError, QuotaExceededError, ValueError),  # ...except these
))
def call_api() -> dict:
    return client.fetch()

ignore_on takes precedence over retry_on, bypasses any configured fallback, and emits a single EventType.FAILURE event. The same option exists on CircuitBreakerConfig so ignored exceptions don't trip the circuit either — see CircuitBreaker.

docs.title: Dynamic Delays (delay_func)
docs.text:
delay_func receives the attempt number and the trigger — the raised exception (exception-driven retries) or the raw return value (retry_on_result retries) — and returns the delay in seconds. Return None to fall back to the configured exponential backoff. Non-None returns are clamped to [0, max_delay].

def delay_from_error(attempt: int, trigger) -> Optional[float]:
    if isinstance(trigger, RateLimitError):
        return trigger.retry_after          # server told us how long to wait
    return None                             # exponential backoff for everything else

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=4, delay=1.0, delay_func=delay_from_error))
def call_api() -> dict:
    return client.fetch()

The most common use — honoring HTTP Retry-After headers on 429 responses — ships ready-made in pyresilience.contrib.http:

from pyresilience.contrib.http import retry_on_status, retry_after_delay

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(
    max_attempts=4,
    retry_on_result=retry_on_status(429, 503),
    delay_func=retry_after_delay(max_wait=60.0),
))
def call_api():
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com")

docs.title: Events
Retry Budget
docs.text:
A retry budget limits the total number of retries across all decorated functions, preventing cascading retry storms during widespread outages.

from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig, RetryBudgetConfig, RetryBudget

budget = RetryBudget(RetryBudgetConfig(max_retries=100, refill_rate=10))

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, retry_budget=budget))
def call_service_a():
    return requests.get("https://a.example.com").json()

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, retry_budget=budget))
def call_service_b():
    return requests.get("https://b.example.com").json()
Parameter Type Default Description max_retries int 100 Maximum retry tokens in the budget pool refill_rate float 10 Tokens refilled per second

When the budget is exhausted, retry attempts are skipped and the last exception propagates immediately. The budget refills over time at the configured rate.

This is especially useful in microservice architectures where many functions share the same downstream dependency — if the dependency is down, the budget prevents all functions from retrying simultaneously.

docs.title: Exponential Backoff (default)
docs.text:
RetryConfig(delay=1.0, backoff_factor=2.0)
# Delays: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, ...

docs.title: Linear Backoff
docs.text:
RetryConfig(delay=1.0, backoff_factor=1.0)
# Delays: 1s, 1s, 1s, 1s, ...

docs.title: Aggressive Backoff
docs.text:
RetryConfig(delay=0.1, backoff_factor=3.0, max_delay=30.0)
# Delays: 0.1s, 0.3s, 0.9s, 2.7s, 8.1s, 24.3s, 30s (capped), ...

docs.title: TimeLimiter (Timeout)
docs.text: The time limiter pattern enforces a maximum execution time for each call. If the call exceeds the timeout, it is cancelled and a TimeoutError is raised.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
By default the timeout wraps each individual call attempt (not the total time across retries). An overall deadline and a stream idle limit can be added on top:

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3), timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=5))

Attempt 1: [─── 5s max ───] TIMEOUT!
Attempt 2: [── 3s ──] SUCCESS!

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Mode How it works Sync Runs the function in a thread pool, uses future.result(timeout=...) with best-effort thread cancellation Async Uses asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout=...)

Thread Cancellation (Sync)

On CPython, when a sync function exceeds its timeout, pyresilience uses ctypes.pythonapi.PyThreadState_SetAsyncExc for best-effort thread interruption. This raises an exception in the worker thread so it can clean up. However, blocking C extensions (e.g., socket.recv() without a timeout) cannot be interrupted. The original exception chain is preserved via from exc.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from pyresilience import TimeoutConfig

config = TimeoutConfig(
    seconds=30.0,              # Maximum execution time
    per_attempt=True,          # True = per attempt, False = total deadline
    total_seconds=None,        # Overall deadline on top of the per-attempt limit
    stream_idle_seconds=None,  # Max gap between items of a streamed result
)
Parameter Type Default Description seconds float 30.0 Maximum time in seconds before the call is aborted per_attempt bool True Whether seconds applies per attempt or as a total deadline total_seconds Optional[float] None Overall deadline for all attempts and retry waits, enforced together with the per-attempt seconds. Requires per_attempt=True stream_idle_seconds Optional[float] None Idle limit for results that are iterators or async iterators pool_size int 4 Thread pool size for sync timeouts

docs.title: Basic Timeout
docs.text:
from pyresilience import resilient, TimeoutConfig

@resilient(timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=5.0))
def slow_operation() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://slow-api.example.com").json()

docs.title: With Retry
docs.text:
Each retry attempt gets its own timeout:

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, delay=1.0),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=10),
)
def call_api() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

Total maximum time: 3 attempts * 10s timeout + 2 delays = ~32s worst case.

docs.title: Async Timeout
docs.text:
@resilient(timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=5.0))
async def async_fetch(url: str) -> dict:
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get(url) as resp:
            return await resp.json()

docs.title: Per-Attempt vs Total Deadline
docs.text:
By default (per_attempt=True), each retry attempt gets the full timeout:

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3), timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=5))

Attempt 1: [─── 5s max ───] TIMEOUT!
Attempt 2: [─── 5s max ───] TIMEOUT!
Attempt 3: [── 3s ──] SUCCESS!
Total: up to 15s + delays

With per_attempt=False, the timeout is a total deadline shared across all attempts:

@resilient(retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3), timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=5, per_attempt=False))

Attempt 1: [── 3s ──] TIMEOUT!
Attempt 2: [─ 1.5s ─] TIMEOUT! (remaining budget)
Attempt 3: TIMEOUT! (no budget left)
Total: 5s max

Use per_attempt=False when you have a strict SLA and need to bound total latency:

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, delay=0.5),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=5.0, per_attempt=False),
)
def call_with_deadline() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

docs.title: Per-Attempt Limit and Overall Deadline Together
docs.text:
total_seconds bounds the whole call while seconds still bounds every attempt. Each attempt gets min(seconds, time left):

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=4, delay=1.0),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=10.0, total_seconds=30.0),
)
def call_api() -> dict:
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com").json()

seconds=10, total_seconds=30

Attempt 1: [─── 10s max ───] TIMEOUT!          wait 1s
Attempt 2: [─── 10s max ───] TIMEOUT!          wait 2s
Attempt 3: [── 7s left ──]   TIMEOUT!          next wait (4s) does not fit
           raise ResilienceTimeoutError("... exceeded total timeout budget of 30.0s")
Total: 30s max

When the time left cannot cover the next retry wait, the call stops retrying at once and raises ResilienceTimeoutError, chained from the last error. It does not sleep past the deadline. The same applies to per_attempt=False. A fallback is used instead when fallback_on matches the timeout or the error that was being retried; a handler set up for the retried error receives that error.

Two details: an attempt that is cut short by the deadline emits one TIMEOUT event, whose detail names the time the attempt really had. And with a bulkhead, the wait for a slot after a retry sleep is bounded by BulkheadConfig.max_wait, not by the deadline; if the deadline has passed when the slot is granted, the call stops without another attempt.

With retry_on_result, the last result is returned when the budget runs out, as it is when attempts run out.

The deadline covers the attempts and the retry waits. It does not cover the wait for rate-limit capacity or a bulkhead slot before the first attempt, and it does not bound fallback alternatives: give an alternative its own @resilient(timeout=...).

docs.title: Stream Idle Timeout
docs.text:
A call that returns a stream finishes quickly; the waiting happens while the stream is consumed. stream_idle_seconds bounds the wait for the first item and between two items:

@resilient(timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=30.0, stream_idle_seconds=15.0))
async def stream_completion(prompt: str):
    return client.stream(prompt)   # an async iterator

async for chunk in await stream_completion("hello"):
    ...   # ResilienceTimeoutError if no chunk arrives for 15s
  • Applies when the function returns an iterator, generator, async iterator or async generator. Other results are returned unchanged.
  • The wait for the first item is the time to first token.
  • Each sync stream is read by its own daemon thread, started with the first item, so any number of streams can run at once. A read that is abandoned keeps that thread busy, and the underlying stream open, until the read returns.
  • The body of a sync stream runs in a copy of the caller's context, taken at the first item: context variables set by the caller are visible in it, changes made inside it do not reach the caller.
  • Because that body runs in another thread, objects tied to the thread that created them cannot be used in it: a sqlite3 connection opened by the caller raises ProgrammingError, and threading.local values set by the caller are not there. Create such objects inside the stream.
  • Handing each item of a sync stream from one thread to the other costs far more than the async guard (see Performance). It does not matter for network streams; think twice for streams of many small in-memory items.
  • After a timeout the stream is finished. Retries and fallbacks do not cover a stream that already started.
  • with / async with, close(), aclose() and other attributes are passed through to the wrapped stream.

docs.title: When to Use pyresilience
docs.text:
Use pyresilience when you need:

  • Multiple resilience patterns working together
  • A single, clean API instead of stacking decorators
  • Consistent observability across all patterns
  • Shared circuit breaker state across functions
  • Production presets for common integration patterns
  • Retry, circuit breaker, timeout, fallback, bulkhead, rate limiter, or cache — individually or combined

docs.title: Your First Resilient Function
docs.text:
The simplest usage — add retry with default settings:

import requests
from pyresilience import resilient

@resilient
def fetch_data():
    return requests.get("https://api.example.com/data").json()

When used without arguments, @resilient applies default retry (3 attempts, 1s delay, exponential backoff with jitter).

docs.title: Configuring Patterns
docs.text:
Pass configuration objects to enable specific patterns:

import requests
from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig, TimeoutConfig

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, delay=0.5),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=10),
)
def call_api(endpoint: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(endpoint).json()

docs.title: Async Support
docs.text:
The decorator auto-detects async functions — no changes needed:

import aiohttp
from pyresilience import resilient, RetryConfig, TimeoutConfig

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=5),
)
async def async_fetch(url: str) -> dict:
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get(url) as resp:
            return await resp.json()

docs.title: Full Example
docs.text:
Combine all patterns for production-grade resilience:

from pyresilience import (
    resilient,
    RetryConfig,
    TimeoutConfig,
    CircuitBreakerConfig,
    FallbackConfig,
    BulkheadConfig,
    RateLimiterConfig,
    CacheConfig,
)

@resilient(
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, delay=0.5, backoff_factor=2.0),
    timeout=TimeoutConfig(seconds=10),
    circuit_breaker=CircuitBreakerConfig(failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30),
    fallback=FallbackConfig(handler=lambda e: {"error": str(e), "cached": True}),
    bulkhead=BulkheadConfig(max_concurrent=20),
    rate_limiter=RateLimiterConfig(max_calls=100, period=60.0),
    cache=CacheConfig(max_size=256, ttl=300.0),
)
def get_user_profile(user_id: int) -> dict:
    import requests
    return requests.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}").json()

This single decorator:

  1. Checks the cache for a previously stored result
  2. Checks the circuit breaker — fails fast if the service is down
  3. Checks the rate limiter — respects API rate limits
  4. Acquires a bulkhead slot — limits to 20 concurrent calls
  5. Retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff on failure
  6. Times out each attempt after 10 seconds
  7. Returns a fallback value if all else fails
  8. Stores successful results in the cache

docs.title: Using Presets
docs.text:
For common integration patterns, use opinionated presets instead of manual config:

from pyresilience import resilient
from pyresilience.presets import http_policy, db_policy

@resilient(**http_policy())
def call_api(url: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(url).json()

@resilient(**db_policy())
def query_db(sql: str) -> list:
    return cursor.execute(sql).fetchall()

See Presets for all available presets and their defaults.
